question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't contain the rule that would decide a retaliation challenge on 1 November 2019. They do cover the repair-request steps that led up to your notice.

**Which version applies:** The only retrieved Act version in force on 1 November 2019 is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Authorised Version No. 088, dated 2 July 2019) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The other versions I retrieved (2020, 2022, 2025, 2026) are not in force on your date, so I have not used them.

**What the 2019 version says about repairs:**
- For non-urgent repairs, you must give the landlord written notice that repairs are required [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- If the landlord hasn't carried out those repairs within 14 days of that notice, you may apply to the Director to investigate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- After the Director's report, you may apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring specified repairs. That application must be made within 60 days of receiving the report [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- For urgent repairs, you may arrange them yourself if you have taken reasonable steps to get the landlord to do them immediately and the landlord can't or won't. The landlord must then reimburse the reasonable cost, up to $1000 or a prescribed amount [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- If you think the notice is linked to your repair request, the 2019 version I retrieved doesn't say whether that makes the notice invalid, how to challenge it, or what time limit applies. The notice-to-vacate provisions in the 2019 version are not in the excerpts I retrieved. Later versions contain retaliation provisions, but those don't apply on 1 November 2019, so I haven't relied on them [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover:**
- Whether a notice to vacate on a month-to-month tenancy must give a minimum period, and what that period is.
- The required form, reasons, or supporting documents for a notice to vacate in 2019.
- Whether a notice given after a repair request is invalid, and how to challenge it.
- Whether leaking fixtures count as "urgent repairs". The definition is in s 3(1), which I did not retrieve.

**Facts that will decide your position:**
1. **Form of your repair request.** Was it in writing, and what date was it given? Non-urgent repair steps depend on written notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Whether the repairs were done.** Did the landlord finish them within 14 days, and did you have any other exchanges that show the timing?
3. **Whether the leaks were urgent.** This depends on the s 3(1) definition, which I did not retrieve.
4. **The notice itself.** Its stated reason, termination date, form, and how it was delivered. These need checking against the 2019 Act, which I could not retrieve.
5. **Your tenancy terms.** Whether there is any term that affects notice.

**What you can do now:**
- Keep copies of your repair request, any reply, and the notice, with dates.
- If the repairs are still outstanding after 14 days from a written notice, you can apply to the Director under s 74 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- Get urgent advice on challenging the notice, and check the 2019 Act's text on notices to vacate and retaliation, which these documents do not include.

must-mention.reason: No: the answer misses every required point. It never says a no-reason notice is allowed with at least 120 days notice; it lists the minimum notice period as something the documents don't cover. It never says a notice given in response to a repair request has no effect; it says the 2019 version doesn't say whether such a notice is invalid. It never says the tenant can challenge at VCAT within 60 days; its only 60-day limit is for a Tribunal repair application after a Director's report.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the landlord had to give a reason; it lists 'The required form, reasons, or supporting documents for a notice to vacate in 2019' as not covered. Its only deadlines are '14 days' for the landlord to do repairs and 'within 60 days of receiving the report' for a repair-order application, and it says the retrieved version 'doesn't say ... what time limit applies' to challenging the notice.

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version No. 088, dated 2 July 2019)' and takes every rule it applies from that in-force version, mentioning later versions (e.g., 97-109aa110) only to say they don't apply and are not relied on.

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
**Short answer:** Possibly, but it depends on facts you haven't given me. The Act in force on 1 October 2025 bans an agent from *soliciting* a higher rent offer, and it bans misleading conduct about rent. It does not, in the version I found, cover accepting an unsolicited higher offer, and it says nothing about withdrawal emails.

## Which version applies

The version in force on 1 October 2025 is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version v110, dated 6 August 2025 (file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf") [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). I did not use the later version dated 25 November 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), because it postdates your date. The Regulations I retrieved are also dated after 1 October 2025 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), so I can't tell you what the Regulations said on your date.

## What the law says (v110)

- **Fixed advertised rent:** Premises must be advertised or offered with the rent as a fixed amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **No soliciting higher offers:** A provider or agent must not "solicit or otherwise invite an offer of an amount of rent that is higher than the advertised amount" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person or 300 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Misleading rent representations:** A provider or agent who promotes or advertises rented premises must not make a false or misleading representation about the rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Separately, a provider must not induce someone to enter an agreement by misleading or deceptive conduct, including a false or misleading representation about "the rent payable under the agreement" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Tribunal orders:** The Act notes that the Tribunal may make orders on an application for a contravention of the misleading-conduct section [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Discrimination:** If the refusal was based on a protected attribute, the Act notes that a person may apply to the Tribunal for compensation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Your facts don't suggest this, so I haven't assessed it.

## What the law does not cover

- **Accepting an unsolicited higher offer:** The v110 text has no ban on accepting an uninvited higher offer. A later version adds that rule [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). I have not applied it to your situation, because it wasn't in force on 1 October 2025.
- **Withdrawal emails:** The retrieved documents contain no rule about how applications are withdrawn, closed, or notified.
- **Evidence:** The documents don't say what evidence a renter should keep.
- **Procedure and time limits:** The retrieved text doesn't set out how to apply to the Tribunal or any deadline.

## Facts that will decide it

1. Did the agent or provider themselves ask for, or invite, a higher offer? Or did the higher offer come unprompted?
2. Was the advertised rent stated as a fixed amount?
3. Did the withdrawal email say something false about you, and did it lead to the property being re-let or re-priced?
4. Was the refusal or withdrawal based on a protected attribute?

## Evidence to keep

The documents don't list evidence. These are general practical suggestions, not drawn from the Act:

- The advertisement, with the stated rent and any "fixed amount" wording.
- Your application and the withdrawal email, including full headers and dates.
- Any messages about the rent, the higher offer, or the re-listing, plus screenshots of the current listing.
- A dated note of your conversations with the agent.

must-mention.reason: No. The answer never says that relisting the property at a higher fixed rent is not illegal by itself. It covers the ban on soliciting higher offers, the absence of a ban on accepting unsolicited offers on that date ("The v110 text has no ban on accepting an uninvited higher offer"), and the lack of any rule on withdrawal emails, but it does not address whether the re-listing at a higher rent was lawful in itself.

must-not-say.reason: Yes — none of the three failing claims is asserted: the answer says "The v110 text has no ban on accepting an uninvited higher offer" and attributes that rule only to a later version it explicitly did not apply. It never calls relisting at a higher rent illegal by itself, and it never says the applicant can force the agent to rent the property to them.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "Authorised Version v110, dated 6 August 2025 (file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf")" and takes every rule it applies from that version. It mentions the later v111 only to note a rule added afterwards that it expressly does not apply. It also cites the later Regulations only to say it cannot rely on them, so no rule comes from a version that was not in force.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the law in force on 15 October 2026, the owner cannot simply refuse. They must not unreasonably refuse, and if they want to refuse, they must go to the Tribunal within 14 days. Whether they can refuse depends on facts you haven't given me, mainly whether they applied to the Tribunal in time.

I'm relying on the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, the version dated 13 October 2026 (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf") [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Act's pet provisions are in Division 5B, sections 71A–71E [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What the Act says**

- A renter may keep a pet if the provider has consented in writing, or the Tribunal has ordered it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The request must be made in the form approved by the Director, and given to the provider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Your use of the official form meets the form requirement.
- The provider "must not unreasonably refuse to consent" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The provider is taken to have consented unless, within 14 days after receiving the request, they apply to the Tribunal under section 71D [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Applying this to your situation**

- **Timing:** Three weeks before 15 October is about 24–25 September, so the 14-day window closed around 8–9 October. If the owner did not apply to the Tribunal by then, the Act says they are taken to have consented [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The agent's refusal is not, on the text, the same as a Tribunal application.
- **Reasonableness:** If the owner did apply, the Tribunal decides whether it is reasonable to refuse. It may consider the type of pet, the character of the premises and its appliances and fittings, whether refusal is permitted under any other Act, prescribed matters, and any other relevant matter [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents do not mention allergies or how often the owner visits, so I can't say whether either reason would be accepted.
- **Not covered:** The documents don't address whether the owner's allergy is a valid reason, or whether any other law (such as building or owners' corporation rules) bars dogs in your building.

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Check for a Tribunal application.** Ask the agent or owner whether they applied to the Tribunal under section 71D, and when. If they did not within 14 days, the Act says consent is taken to have been given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Get written consent.** Ask for written confirmation that the dog is allowed, since section 71A refers to written consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **If the owner did apply,** the Tribunal may allow the dog, refuse consent, or exclude the pet. Until an order is made, the Act's default rule applies [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Know the risk if you keep a dog without consent.** If the Tribunal excludes the pet and you don't comply after 14 days, the owner may give a notice to vacate with at least 28 days to leave [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Facts that decide the outcome:** whether an application was made within 14 days; the type and size of the dog; the character of the apartment and its fittings; and whether any other Act or rule restricts pets. The documents don't cover the last point. This is general information, not legal advice. For a firm answer, you can contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered, and the hardest one is met by the words 'the 14-day window closed around 8–9 October. If the owner did not apply to the Tribunal by then, the Act says they are taken to have consented', with the next step 'Ask the agent or owner whether they applied to the Tribunal under section 71D' also present.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the agent's refusal is final, that the renter must apply to VCAT, or that the allergy settles the matter; it says the owner "must go to the Tribunal within 14 days," that "the agent's refusal is not, on the text, the same as a Tribunal application," and that "I can't say whether either reason would be accepted."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as 'the version dated 13 October 2026 (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf")' with link 97-109aa115, which is Authorised Version No. 115, the version in force on 15 October 2026, and every rule it applies is sourced only from that version.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the version of the Act in force on 1 October 2025, a notice to vacate stays in place until a formal notice of withdrawal is given. The buyer pulling out does not, by itself, withdraw it. The documents don't say whether the notice still works once the sale has fallen through, so whether you must leave depends on facts I don't have.

**The law in force on 1 October 2025**

The relevant version is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version v110, dated 6 August 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The Act says a notice to vacate "is withdrawn only if a notice of withdrawal is given." That notice must be in writing, signed by the person who gave the notice, and signed by the person to whom it was given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). So the landlord's silence or the sale falling through does not withdraw it. Only a signed withdrawal notice does, and it needs your signature as well.

A landlord can give a sale-based notice under section 91ZZB if the premises are, immediately after the termination date, "to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The notice must give at least 60 days' notice of the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Where a contract of sale is conditional, the notice must be given within 14 days after the last condition is satisfied. If the contract is not conditional in that way, it must be given within 14 days after the contract is entered into [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover**

- **Whether the notice stays valid after the sale collapses.** Section 91ZZB is framed around a sale happening or being offered [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The retrieved documents don't say whether a landlord who no longer sells must withdraw, or whether the notice lapses on its own.
- **What the Tribunal would do if the landlord applied for a possession order.** The 2025 excerpts I retrieved don't include the Part 7 possession-order provisions, so I can't say from them what VCAT must decide.

**What you can do**

1. **Check the notice's validity.** A notice to vacate is not valid unless it is in the relevant prescribed form, addressed to you, signed, states the reasons, comes with documentary evidence approved by the Director for sale-based notices, and specifies the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
2. **Challenge it within 30 days.** On or before a possession-order hearing, you may apply to the Tribunal challenging the notice's validity. The application must be made within 30 days after the notice was given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
3. **Ask the landlord in writing to withdraw it.** A withdrawal only takes effect if both you and the landlord sign a notice of withdrawal [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). You can't withdraw it on your own.
4. **Get advice promptly.** The 2025 Regulations' form says that if you want to challenge a notice you should seek legal advice as soon as possible [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Note that this document is dated 25 November 2025, after your date, so I haven't relied on it for any rule.

**Facts that decide the answer**

- The date the notice was given (this sets your 30-day challenge window).
- The termination date, which must be at least 60 days after the notice was given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- Whether the notice was given within 14 days of the sale contract (or of the last condition being met) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- Whether the notice was in the prescribed form and came with the required documentary evidence [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- Whether the landlord has said in writing that they will withdraw it.

If the notice is valid and not withdrawn, the documents indicate you would need to leave by the termination date. Whether a sale that has collapsed still supports the notice is a question the retrieved documents don't answer. Please get advice from a tenancy service such as Consumer Affairs Victoria (1300 558 181) or a community legal centre.

**Sources**
[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version v110, dated 6 August 2025 (rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf).
[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version v005, dated 25 November 2025 (rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf). Not in force on 1 October 2025.

must-mention.reason: No: the answer covers the 60-day minimum, withdrawal only by a written notice signed by both parties, and next steps (a signed withdrawal or a VCAT challenge within 30 days), but it misses the first point. It never explains that the outcome depends on which ground the notice states and the evidence attached: premises to be offered for sale with vacant possession, which survives the buyer pulling out, versus a signed contract of sale. It treats the 14-day contract timing as applying to every sale notice and leaves the collapsed-sale question unanswered.

None of the failure conditions is asserted: the answer says "The buyer pulling out does not, by itself, withdraw it," states that a withdrawal "only takes effect if both you and the landlord sign a notice of withdrawal," and gives the minimum period as "at least 60 days' notice of the termination date."

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the law in force on 1 October 2025, an email saying rent is going up is not, by itself, a valid rent increase. You probably do not have to pay the higher rent unless the agent gives you a proper notice. The documents don't give a start date for you, so the exact timing depends on what the agent sent.

**The governing versions**

- **Act:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file labelled Authorised Version v110, dated 6 August 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Regulations:** *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version v004, dated 1 July 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

Other versions in the search results are dated after 1 October 2025, so I have not relied on them.

**What the law says**

- A rent increase needs a notice. The rental provider must give at least 60 days' notice in the prescribed form of a proposed rent increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The notice may provide for only one increase. It must state the amount of the increase, the method used to calculate it, and tell you of your right to apply to the Director within 30 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The prescribed form is Form 5. It must include the method of calculation, and the increase cannot be greater than the amount that method produces [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- A rent increase that does not comply with these requirements is invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The rental provider must not increase rent more than once every 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). In a fixed-term agreement, rent cannot be increased before the term ends unless the agreement provides for it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**What the law does not cover in your situation**

The documents do not say whether an informal email from an agent can ever count as the notice. They also do not say what happens if an agent's email contains some, but not all, of the required details. Form 5 allows notice by email only if the renter has consented [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Form 5 also says the rental provider's name "cannot be the agent's name", although the agent's address may be used for service [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**Facts that decide the answer**

1. Whether the agent sent a Form 5 (or a notice containing its required contents).
2. Whether the notice gives at least 60 days before the increase starts.
3. Whether your agreement is fixed-term, and whether it provides for an increase.
4. When the rent was last increased. The 12-month rule applies.
5. Whether the notice was properly given to you, including by email only if you consented.

**What you can do**

- Ask the agent in writing for a proper Form 5 notice, if one has not been sent.
- If a notice is given, you may apply in writing to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria within 30 days after the notice is given to investigate whether the proposed rent is excessive [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- You may also apply to VCAT for an order declaring the proposed rent excessive. This must be made within 30 days after receiving the Director's report, or within 30 days after the notice is given if there is no report [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- Form 5 says you will need to pay the increased amount from the date on the notice unless VCAT decides otherwise [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). This applies only to a valid notice, so do not assume you must pay the increase before one is properly given.

**A later change to note**

A later version of the Regulations, dated 25 November 2025, changes Form 5 to require 90 days' notice [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). That version is not in force on 1 October 2025 and does not apply to your situation today. Note also that the documents I found do not include a later version of the Act setting out a different rule on rent increases.

*This is general information from the retrieved documents, not legal advice. For advice on your specific lease, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or a community legal centre.*

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered: it names Form 5 as the prescribed form, requires at least 60 days' notice, and says 'an email saying rent is going up is not, by itself, a valid rent increase. You probably do not have to pay the higher rent unless the agent gives you a proper notice' and 'A rent increase that does not comply with these requirements is invalid'. That is the hardest point, and despite the mild 'probably' its direction is clear. It also gives next steps: asking the agent in writing for a proper Form 5, and applying to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria once a notice is given.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved law says you must tell the owner in writing about the damage. It does not allow you to arrange repairs secretly and then leave it there. The documents also don't address insurance.

**Version used:** Act: *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (file labelled v115, dated 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Regulations: *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (file labelled v005, dated 25 November 2025) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). I did not use the earlier Act versions [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**What the law says**

- **You must notify the owner.** A renter must give written notice to the owner "as soon as practicable after becoming aware of" damage to the rented premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations say the same: where damage occurs, the renter must notify the rental provider in writing [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **The owner can require you to repair it.** If damage is caused by a renter's failure to comply with the duty to take care, the owner may give a written repair notice. It must state the nature of the damage and that it was caused by the renter's failure to take care. If the owner wants you to repair it, the notice must require repair at your expense within 14 days, and it must say that if you don't repair it in a tradesman-like manner within that period, the owner may do so at your expense [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **If you don't repair it, the owner can.** If you haven't repaired the damage in a proper and tradesman-like manner within 14 days, the owner may repair it at your expense. You are liable for the reasonable costs if the owner gives you written particulars of the cost, and you must reimburse within 14 days after the repairs are completed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Who can do the work.** Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, both urgent and non-urgent [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). So any tradesperson you use should be suitably qualified.
- **Urgent repairs don't appear to apply.** The urgent repairs provisions cover things like failure of essential services or appliances for hot water, cooking, heating or laundering [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The documents don't list chewed skirting boards as urgent, so I can't say the urgent repairs route applies.

**What the documents don't cover**

- **Doing the repair without telling the owner:** The documents don't expressly say whether a renter can privately repair their own damage without notice. What they do require is written notice of the damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A repair done in secret would not replace that notice.
- **Insurance:** The documents don't say anything about the owner's insurance, or whether your damage would affect it. You would need to check the owner's policy or ask the owner or insurer.

**Facts that decide the practical outcome**

- Whether you have already told the owner about the damage in writing.
- Whether the owner has already given a repair notice or a breach of duty notice.
- Whether the dog was allowed at the property. The documents I retrieved don't deal with pets beyond consent provisions, so I can't say more on this.
- What your residential rental agreement says about repairs and damage. I didn't retrieve it.

**Practical next step:** Give the owner written notice of the damage now, before you move out, and ask whether they want you to arrange a suitably qualified person to repair it. Keep the quote, invoice and proof of payment. That keeps you on the path the Act sets out, and it avoids a repair notice and a possible dispute at the end of the tenancy.

It also applies rules from v005 as current law: notifying in writing, repairs by a suitably qualified person, and the scope of urgent repairs. That means it relies on a version that was not in force on that date.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I retrieved do not set a limit on the number of circuits a rental needs, or on how many power points can share one. The rule that applies from 29 March 2023 is about protective devices, not circuit count.

**Which version applies**

Your question is dated 1 March 2023. The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 version in force then is the one dated 1 June 2022 (file "rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf") [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The retrieved text does not show an Authorised Version number, so I can't give one. A later amendment table lists no amendment between 1 June 2022 and the 2024 changes [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The retrieved Residential Tenancies Act 1997 versions are dated 2025 and 2026 [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), so none is confirmed as in force on 1 March 2023. I can't say what the Act required on that date.

**What the rule says**

- The electrical safety standard starts "On and from 29 March 2023," which is 28 days after your date. It is not yet in force on 1 March 2023 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- From that date, all power outlets and lighting circuits must be connected to a switchboard-type circuit breaker complying with AS/NZS 3000, and a switchboard-type residual current device complying with AS/NZS 3190, AS/NZS 61008.1 or AS/NZS 61009.1 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

**What it does not cover**

The regulation does not specify how many circuits a rental must have, how many outlets can share a circuit, or how much load a circuit must carry. It also does not address your breaker tripping when the kettle and heater run together. The documents don't say whether that trip indicates a breach.

**Heater requirement (only if relevant)**

Until 28 March 2023, a fixed heater in good working order must be in the main living area for a Class 1 building. From 29 March 2023, an energy efficient fixed heater in good working order must be installed there [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). This concerns the heater itself, not the circuit it runs on.

**What you can ask for**

Under the standard, you can ask your landlord (rental provider) to make sure the outlets and lighting circuits are connected to a compliant circuit breaker and residual current device. This applies from 29 March 2023 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The documents do not say:

- how quickly the landlord must respond
- who pays for the work
- what steps apply if they refuse, or how VCAT would be involved

I can't cover those from the retrieved documents.

**Facts that would change the answer**

- Whether the building is Class 1 or Class 2, since the heating rules differ [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- Whether the rental agreement was entered into before or after 29 March 2023. The electrical rule applies from that date regardless, but I have not confirmed the agreement-date rules for other standards in the version in force on your date.
- Whether your heater is a fixed heater.
- Whether the breaker and residual current device already comply, which an electrician could check.

**General advice (not from the documents)**

A tripping breaker usually means the circuit is overloaded. A licensed electrician can check the wiring and load and advise whether the circuit needs changes. It's worth putting your request to the landlord in writing and keeping a record.

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. The no-circuit-count rule is stated as "The documents I retrieved do not set a limit on the number of circuits a rental needs." The hardest point, the next step, is covered by "you can ask your landlord (rental provider) to make sure the outlets and lighting circuits are connected to a compliant circuit breaker and residual current device" together with "put your request to the landlord in writing and keeping a record." That is a reasonable repair request consistent with the law.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer sets no minimum number of circuits ('The regulation does not specify how many circuits a rental must have, how many outlets can share a circuit') and says the RCD/circuit breaker standard is not yet in force ('It is not yet in force on 1 March 2023').

version-cited.reason: No. The answer names the Regulations' in-force version correctly as "the one dated 1 June 2022" (link 21-3sra002), but it never names Residential Tenancies Act 1997 Authorised Version No. 101. It cites only versions 115, 111 and 110 ("97-109aa115", "97-109aa111", "97-109aa110") and says "none is confirmed as in force on 1 March 2023", so a required document is left out with its in-force version.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I found don't say whether a private rooming house operator may charge for coin-operated washing machines. They have no rule that expressly allows or bans this. The rules that do apply depend on who runs the house and how the charge is set up.

I'm applying the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as it stood on 15 October 2026, the Authorised Version dated 13 October 2026 (v115) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Electricity, gas and water charges:** An operator may charge for these only if they are separately metered and the operator pays the supplier. The charge "must not be more than the charge made by the relevant supplier" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This section does not cover washing machines.
- **Charges for services:** If an operator charges for services, it must give the resident "a separate schedule of the amount relating to the services" before the resident moves in. If the resident uses those services, the operator must give "an itemised account showing the resident's individual use of the services" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Service charges by public housing bodies:** Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency may impose a service charge for laundry services in a declared rooming house, but only if "it is not possible or practicable to accurately measure the use" of that service. The charge "must not exceed the cost of providing the service" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This power does not extend to private operators.
- **Washing machine provision:** The Rooming House Standards require, from 26 February 2024, "a washing machine" for every 12 or fewer residents, in good working order [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). The copy I found is dated 1 December 2024, and it does not say whether a charge may be made for using it.
- **Repairs:** Urgent repairs include "failure or breakdown of any essential service or appliance provided for hot water, cooking, heating or laundering supplied by the rooming house operator" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The rooming house operator must carry them out after being notified [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

## What the law does not cover

- It does not say whether coin-operated machines are "services" for the purposes of the schedule and itemised-account rules.
- It does not set a maximum price per wash.
- It does not say whether a coin charge can be set by a private operator.
- It does not say whether a coin-operated machine must be free if the house has a required number of machines.

## What you can do

1. **Ask the operator in writing** whether the machines are a service the operator provides and what it charges.
2. **Ask for the schedule of services** and, if you use the machines, an **itemised account** of your use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the operator has not given you a schedule, that is a point to raise.
3. **If a machine is broken**, notify the operator. If it is not repaired, you may be able to arrange urgent repairs under the regulations [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The rules on this are in the regulations, not the Act.
4. **If the operator is Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency**, you may apply to the Tribunal for an order to withdraw or vary a service charge [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Facts that would decide the answer

- Who runs the house: a private operator, Homes Victoria, or a registered housing agency.
- Whether the house is declared under section 19(2) or (3) of the Act.
- Whether the charge is a fee for machine use or a utility charge.
- Whether you live in a shared room.
- Whether you received a schedule of services before moving in.

If the operator is private and the documents I have don't cover coin charges, you may need to check with Consumer Affairs Victoria, which the regulations point to for more information [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

---

**Sources:**
[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version v115, dated 13 October 2026.
[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023, Authorised Version v002, dated 1 December 2024.
[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version v009, dated 30 June 2026.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are stated: the washing machine standard ('a washing machine' for every 12 or fewer residents, in good working order); that the law does not require the machines to be free ('It does not say whether a coin-operated machine must be free'); the pre-move-in schedule ('must give the resident "a separate schedule of the amount relating to the services" before the resident moves in'); and the next step ('Ask for the schedule of services').

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer never says the machines must be free or that no rules apply, and it limits the cost cap to Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency, stating 'This power does not extend to private operators.'

Deleting that material would change the answer's substance.

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
**Short answer:** The advertising rule I found is not in the Act version in force on 1 October 2025, so the documents don't show that advertising the mould was prohibited on that date. A photo alone also doesn't prove a breach of the mould standard.

## What the law in force on 1 October 2025 says

**Advertising:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110 (dated 6 August 2025), is the version in force on that date. Its text on advertising premises that don't meet the rental minimum standards is not in the excerpt I retrieved [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). A later version (Authorised Version No. 111, dated 25 November 2025) contains an advertising provision, and it was inserted by No. 6/2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say when No. 6/2025 commenced, so I can't confirm whether that provision applied on 1 October 2025. I haven't applied it here. If you need to know whether it applied on that date, check the commencement details for No. 6/2025.

**Mould standard:** The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 004 (dated 1 July 2025, per the file name), is the regulation version in force on that date. Schedule 4, clause 8 says: "Each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**What the standard doesn't cover:** It applies only to mould or damp "caused by or related to the building structure." It doesn't cover mould caused by, for example, cleaning or ventilation habits, and the documents don't say how that cause is to be decided.

## Is the photo enough?

The documents don't set out any evidence rules, so I can't say whether a photo is enough. Looking at the standard itself, a photo can show that mould is present. It doesn't show the cause, and the standard requires mould "caused by or related to the building structure." The documents also don't say whether the photos show the actual room at the time the premises were advertised.

## What the renter can do

- **If the renter has moved in:** Under the Act version in force on 1 October 2025, the provider must ensure the premises comply with the rental minimum standards on or before the day the renter enters occupation. If they don't comply on or immediately after that day, the renter may request urgent repairs [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The Act also requires the provider to keep the premises "in good repair" and in a "reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation" [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **If the renter hasn't moved in:** The Act version in force on 1 October 2025 says a renter is not required to enter occupation of premises that are not vacant or not reasonably clean on the agreed day, and is not required to pay rent for the period before they actually move in [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The excerpt doesn't address mould specifically in this situation.
- **Evidence:** Keep the advertisement, the photos, and the date you saw them. Also keep any records of the room's condition. The documents don't state what records are required.

## What decides the answer

- Whether the renter has moved in, and on what date.
- Whether the mould is caused by or related to the building structure.
- Whether the room in the photos is the room in the advertised premises, and when the photos were taken.
- Whether the advertising provision in the later Act version applied on 1 October 2025 (I couldn't confirm this from the documents).

The documents don't cover how a dispute about these facts is decided, such as the Tribunal's process or what evidence it requires.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: the answer quotes the mould standard ('free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure'), states that 'A photo alone also doesn't prove a breach of the mould standard', and gives a next step ('the renter may request urgent repairs'). The hardest point, the photo not proving a breach, is stated plainly and explained as showing presence but not cause.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I found don't set out steps for removing a friend who has moved in. They only cover what happens if your landlord or agent acts because you let someone else occupy the property without consent.

**Version used:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115 (file dated 13 October 2026), is the version in force on 15 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I haven't applied any other version.

## What the law says

- **Sub-letting or assigning without consent:** Your landlord may give you a notice to vacate if you "assigned or sub-let or purported to assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the premises without the residential rental provider's consent." The termination date must be at least 14 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Whether this applies to you depends on facts the documents don't define.** The excerpt doesn't define "sub-let" or "assign." It's unclear whether a friend who lives with you without paying rent, or without taking over any part of the premises, falls within this rule. The key facts are whether your friend pays you any money, whether they have any agreement with you about their stay, and whether they have exclusive use of any part of the home.

## What the law doesn't cover

- The documents don't say how you must ask a friend to leave, how much notice you must give them, or what happens if they refuse.
- They don't say whether you had to tell the agent about the friend moving in.
- They don't cover the friend's rights as a non-party occupant.

## Notice formalities (if your landlord serves you a notice)

For notices under this Division, the notice is not valid unless it is in the prescribed form, addressed to the renter, signed by the giver or their agent, specifies the reason(s), and specifies the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A notice can only be withdrawn by a written notice of withdrawal, signed by both the person who gave the notice and the person it was given to [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The documents show that a renter can challenge the validity of some notices at the Tribunal, but that route applies to notices given under sections 91ZX to 91ZZC, not section 91ZV [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The excerpt doesn't give the process or time limit for challenging a section 91ZV notice.

## What you can do

1. **Ask your friend to leave.** The documents contain no rule for this, so the terms of any arrangement you made with them will matter.
2. **Check the facts that decide your position:** whether your friend pays rent or contributes money, whether they have their own space, and whether the agent has consented.
3. **If the agent serves a notice,** check that it meets the formal requirements above and that the termination date is at least 14 days after it was given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **If you want to end your own tenancy,** the documents I retrieved don't include the text of the notice of intention to vacate provisions, so I can't tell you what that requires.

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the Act in force on 1 November 2019, a notice can be void if it was given in response to your exercise of a renter's right, but the retrieved text does not clearly cover a notice to a periodic renter that follows a repair request. Whether you can challenge this notice depends on the reason and section it gives.

## Which law applies

I used the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088, dated 2 July 2019** [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). A later version dated 4 December 2019 exists [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf), but it is not the law in force on 1 November 2019, so I have not applied it.

The retrieved documents include no Residential Tenancies Regulations version from 2019. The earliest regulations version I found is from 2022 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf), so I cannot tell you what the 2019 Regulations required for the notice form.

## What the 2019 Act says

**Retaliation:**

**Possession:**

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
**Short answer:** On 1 October 2025, the Act prohibited the advertising, soliciting, and inviting of higher rent offers, but the retrieved documents don't show whether you have a remedy for a false withdrawal email or a rent increase after listing. Whether anything was breached depends on facts you haven't given me.

## Which version applies

The version in force on 1 October 2025 is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, version 110, dated 6 August 2025 [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). No retrieved Act version falls between that date and 1 October 2025. The later version 111 (25 November 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) and version 115 (13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) do not apply on your date.

I did not find any version of the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* in force on 1 October 2025. The retrieved regulations are dated 25 November 2025 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) and 30 June 2026 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Reg 14A's application form (Form 3A) applies only "on and after 31 March 2026" [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), so it does not apply to your situation.

## What the law says on 1 October 2025

- **Fixed advertised rent:** A provider or agent must not advertise or offer premises unless the rent is advertised or offered as a fixed amount. The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person or 300 for a body corporate [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Inviting higher offers:** A provider or agent "must not solicit or otherwise invite an offer of an amount of rent that is higher than the advertised amount" (same penalties) [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Accepting unsolicited higher offers:** The 1 October 2025 text I retrieved does not contain a prohibition on *accepting* an unsolicited higher offer. That rule appears in version 111 (25 November 2025), which is a later change and does not apply to your date [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Misleading rent representations:** A provider or agent who advertises rented premises must not make a false or misleading representation about the rent (60 or 300 penalty units) [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Misleading conduct inducing you to enter an agreement:** A provider or agent must not induce a person to enter a residential rental agreement by misleading conduct, including false representations about the rent payable [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents do not cover:**
- They do not say whether a withdrawal email you did not send is legally effective.
- They do not say whether a provider can relist a property at a higher rent after the earlier listing was withdrawn, beyond the rules above.
- They do not set out any evidence requirements for a dispute.

## What you can do

- **Tribunal orders:** The note to section 30E says that section 472(1A) provides for orders the Tribunal may make for a contravention of section 30E [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The retrieved excerpts do not include the text of section 472, so I can't confirm what orders are available.
- **Discrimination compensation:** If the refusal was based on a protected attribute, a note says a person may apply to the Tribunal for compensation under section 210AA [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Nothing you've described suggests this, so it applies only if the facts point that way.

## What to save as evidence

The documents do not state what evidence to keep. The facts that will decide the matter are:

1. **The advertisement:** Did it state a fixed rent amount? You will need a copy or screenshot of the listing as it appeared.
2. **The withdrawal email:** The full email, with its date, sender, and headers.
3. **Your application and all correspondence** with the provider or agent, showing what you did and did not say about withdrawing.
4. **Evidence of the higher offer:** Whether the provider or agent asked for offers above the advertised rent (which section 30F(3) prohibits) or whether someone volunteered a higher offer unprompted. This matters because the 1 October 2025 text does not prohibit accepting unsolicited offers [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
5. **The new listing:** A dated screenshot of the higher advertised rent.

Keeping these items is general good practice, not a requirement from the documents.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the Act in force on 15 October 2026, the owner can't simply refuse. The refusal must be reasonable, and if they did not go to the Tribunal within 14 days of your request, the Act treats them as having consented. The documents don't say whether an allergy or infrequent visits make a refusal reasonable, so the answer depends on facts you haven't given me.

**Version relied on:** The Act is *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", dated 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations are *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file "rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf", dated 25 November 2025 [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Neither file states an Authorised Version number on its face, so I've used the file labels. I found no later version in the results.

**What the law says**

- **Consent is needed.** A renter may keep a pet only if the provider has consented in writing or the Tribunal has ordered it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The request must be on the approved form.** The renter must make the request in the form approved by the Director and give it to the provider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **No unreasonable refusal.** The provider "must not unreasonably refuse to consent" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Deemed consent after 14 days.** The provider is taken to have consented unless, within 14 days after the request, they apply to the Tribunal for an order that refusal is reasonable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Tribunal factors.** The Tribunal may consider the type of pet, the character of the premises, the appliances and fittings, whether refusal is permitted under any Act, any prescribed matters, and "any other matter the Tribunal considers relevant" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Regulations.** The standard agreement form says the rental provider "must not unreasonably refuse a request to keep a pet" [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**What the law does not cover**

- The documents don't define "unreasonably."
- They don't mention allergies, so I can't say whether an owner's allergy is a reasonable ground.
- They don't mention how often an owner visits, so I can't say whether that matters.
- They don't say whether a deemed consent under s 71C(2) counts as "consent in writing" under s 71A(a). Please check this with Consumer Affairs Victoria or the Tribunal if it matters to you.
- They don't set out a renter's remedy if a refusal is unreasonable or made outside the 14-day window.

**Facts that decide the answer**

1. **Date you gave the request.** Three weeks before 15 October 2026 is roughly late September. The 14-day period from that date has probably already ended, but you need the exact date.
2. **Whether the owner (or agent acting for them) lodged a Tribunal application within 14 days.** If they did not, the Act treats consent as given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If they did, the Tribunal decides under s 71E [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Whether you used the Director's approved form and delivered it to the provider** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The agent may have received it, but whether it was delivered as required depends on the facts.
4. **The type of dog and the premises.** These are factors the Tribunal may weigh [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do**

- Check the date you gave the request and whether you have proof of delivery.
- Ask the agent or owner in writing whether they have applied to the Tribunal. If none has been lodged within 14 days, you can point to s 71C(2) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Keep a record of the refusal and its stated reason, including the allergy.
- If the provider makes a Tribunal application, you can present your case on the s 71E factors [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Get advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy service about remedies, which the documents don't cover.

Point 3 is covered by "Ask the agent or owner in writing whether they have applied to the Tribunal." The hardest point, the three-week application, is covered by "The 14-day period from that date has probably already ended" together with "if they did not go to the Tribunal within 14 days of your request, the Act treats them as having consented." question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the version of the Act in force on 1 October 2025, the notice probably stays in effect unless the landlord and you both sign a notice of withdrawal. The retrieved documents don't say whether a notice lapses when a sale falls through, so I can't tell you for certain that you must leave.

**What the law in force on 1 October 2025 says**

The relevant version is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* reprint, version 110, dated 6 August 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[11]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Later versions in the search results (dated 25 November 2025 and 13 October 2026) don't apply to your date, so I haven't relied on them.

- **Sale notices:** A landlord may give a notice to vacate if the premises are to be "sold or offered for sale with vacant possession" immediately after the termination date. If a contract of sale is subject to conditions, the landlord must give the notice within 14 days after the last condition is satisfied. If the contract isn't conditional in that way, the notice must be given within 14 days after the contract is entered into [[11]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Termination date:** The notice must specify a termination date at least 60 days after it is given [[11]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Validity:** The notice must be in the prescribed form, addressed to the renter, signed, state the reasons, specify the termination date, and, for a sale notice, be accompanied by documentary evidence supporting the reason [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Withdrawal:** A notice to vacate "is withdrawn only if a notice of withdrawal is given." The withdrawal must be in writing, signed by the person who gave the notice, and signed by the person it was given to [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). So the landlord's silence doesn't withdraw it, but a withdrawal also needs your signature.
- **Challenging the notice:** You may apply to the Tribunal challenging the validity of a sale notice, and the application must be made within 30 days after the notice is given [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If the Tribunal finds the notice valid, you can't challenge it again unless the Tribunal is satisfied that exceptional circumstances justify reconsideration [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover**

- Whether a sale notice stops having effect when the buyer withdraws. The retrieved provisions for this version don't address it.
- How a landlord gets a possession order or what the Tribunal must check before ordering you to leave. The excerpts I retrieved for this version don't include those provisions.

**Facts that decide the answer**

1. **Date the notice was given.** The 30-day challenge window runs from that date, and it may already have passed.
2. **Whether the landlord had a contract of sale, and when it was entered into or its conditions satisfied.** The 14-day rule depends on this.
3. **The termination date.** It must be at least 60 days after the notice was given.
4. **Whether the notice meets the form and evidence requirements** in the sections above.
5. **Whether your tenancy is fixed-term or periodic**, and any break clauses. I haven't checked the rules that apply to fixed-term agreements, so I can't say how they affect this notice.

**What you can do**

- Check the notice's date, termination date, and form against the requirements above.
- Ask the landlord in writing to sign a notice of withdrawal, and keep a record of the request. Withdrawal requires both signatures, so you'd need to sign it too if they do.
- If you think the notice is invalid, seek advice quickly, because the 30-day challenge period is short.
- If the landlord applies for a possession order, go to the Tribunal and raise the validity of the notice.

This isn't legal advice. A tenancy advice service can check your notice and dates.

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
**Short answer:** On the law in force on 1 October 2025, an emailed statement that rent is going up is not a valid rent increase. A rent increase made without a compliant notice is invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The earliest a valid increase could take effect is at least 60 days after a proper notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## What the law in force on 1 October 2025 says

- **Notice is required.** A rental provider must give the renter at least 60 days' notice, in the prescribed form, of a proposed rent increase. The notice must state the amount of the increase, the method used to calculate it, and the renter's right to apply to the Director within 30 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **A rent increase made in breach of this section is invalid** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Timing limits.** The provider cannot increase rent under a fixed-term agreement before the term ends unless the agreement provides for it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The provider also cannot increase rent at intervals of less than 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Standard-form clauses.** Under the standard agreement's rent adjustment options in the regulations version dated 1 July 2025, the provider must still give written notice of the increase 60 days before the date it takes effect [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). This applies only if your agreement contains one of those clauses.

## What the law does not cover, or what it depends on

- **Whether the email counts as notice.** The documents do not say whether an email can be a notice of rent increase. They require the notice to be in the prescribed form [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Whether your agent's email meets that requirement depends on its content, which you have not given me.
- **The prescribed form.** The retrieved excerpts of the regulations in force on 1 October 2025 do not include the text of the prescribed rent-increase form. I cannot confirm its exact requirements from those documents.
- **Your agreement.** Whether the agreement is fixed-term, whether it has a rent-adjustment clause, when rent last increased, and what the proposed amount and start date are all affect the outcome. These facts are not in your question.
- **Later changes.** Later versions of the regulations, including one dated 25 November 2025, change the notice period to 90 days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Those versions do not apply on 1 October 2025, so I have not used them.

## What you can do or ask

3. **Check the timing.** If a notice is given, the new rent cannot start earlier than 60 days after notice, and not within 12 months of your last increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
4. **Challenge an excessive rent if you receive a notice.** You may apply in writing to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria within 30 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). You may also apply to VCAT for an order declaring the proposed rent excessive, after receiving the Director's report, or, with VCAT's leave, without one [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

If you tell me the agreement type (fixed-term or periodic), your current rent, the proposed new rent and start date, and what the agent's email said, I can work through whether the notice would be valid.
