question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
## Law in force on 1 October 2025

I have used **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110, dated 6 August 2025**—the version in force on the date you gave. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

- The property had to be advertised or offered at a **fixed rent**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- The rental provider or agent must not **solicit or otherwise invite** an offer higher than the advertised rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- Advertising the rent falsely or misleadingly is also prohibited, although that provision applies where the provider or agent is **not acting in trade or commerce**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- The Act does **not** say that every unsolicited higher offer is unlawful: the retrieved version prohibits soliciting or inviting a higher offer, but does not state that merely receiving or accepting an unsolicited offer is prohibited. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- The Act does not contain a rule in the retrieved material requiring an agent to give an applicant reasons for rejecting an application, or specifically regulating an email incorrectly saying that an applicant withdrew. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

Accordingly, you may have a basis to challenge the matter if evidence shows that the agent or provider **invited or solicited** applicants to offer more than the advertised rent, or deliberately used the advertised rent in a misleading way. The fact that another person may have offered more, and that the property was later listed at a higher rent, does **not by itself establish** that a breach occurred. The decisive facts include what the agent said or did, when the rent changed, whether anyone was asked or encouraged to offer more, and whether the original advertisement was misleading. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

You can ask the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) about an application, but the Act’s ordinary provision is for a **renter or residential rental provider**. A person who is not one of those parties may apply only **with VCAT’s leave**, and must show an interest and personal involvement sufficient to justify leave. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

If VCAT accepts the application, it may make orders to restrain conduct breaching the Act, require action, or require compensation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) The retrieved Act does not guarantee that an unsuccessful rental applicant will be awarded the property or offered a lease.

The Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria has functions including monitoring compliance and, where appropriate, investigating disputes between a residential rental provider and a renter. The retrieved provisions do not set out a specific applicant complaint process for this situation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

## Evidence

The retrieved documents do **not** prescribe an evidence checklist for an applicant. Preserve the records that bear on the disputed facts—particularly the original advertised rent, your application and its submission time, the withdrawal email, later versions of the listing, and any written or recorded communication about offering more—without altering them. The documents do not state a particular retention period or required format for those records. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered. On the hardest point, the answer states the Act "prohibits soliciting or inviting a higher offer, but does not state that merely receiving or accepting an unsolicited offer is prohibited." It also says the later higher listing "does not by itself establish that a breach occurred," that the provider or agent "must not solicit or otherwise invite" a higher offer, and that the Act contains no rule "specifically regulating an email incorrectly saying that an applicant withdrew."

must-not-say.reason: Yes: none of the three claims is asserted, since the answer says the higher relisting 'does **not by itself establish** that a breach occurred', that the Act 'does not state that merely receiving or accepting an unsolicited offer is prohibited', and that it 'does not guarantee that an unsuccessful rental applicant will be awarded the property or offered a lease.'

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the required document with its in-force version, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110, dated 6 August 2025', and every rule it applies is cited to that version via the 97-109aa110 link, with no reliance on any earlier or later version.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
## Law in force on 15 October 2026

The applicable document is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, dated 13 October 2026** (“the Act”). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If your request was made using the approved form and given to the residential rental provider, the provider **must not unreasonably refuse** consent to keep the dog. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Act does **not** make the owner’s allergy an automatic ground for refusal. It allows the provider to apply to the Tribunal for an order that refusal is reasonable, and the Tribunal may consider the type of pet, the character and nature of the premises, fixtures and fittings, whether another Act permits refusal, prescribed matters and any other relevant matter. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The provider is taken to have consented unless, **within 14 days** after receiving the request, it applies to the Tribunal under section 71D. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Three weeks is 21 days, so if no such Tribunal application was made within that 14-day period, the Act says consent is deemed. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Act does not state that how often the owner visits determines whether an allergy is a reasonable ground; it says the Tribunal may consider any relevant matter. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can ask or do

Ask the agent in writing whether the residential rental provider made a Tribunal application **within 14 days of receiving your request**, and ask for its details. If no timely application was made, the Act says the provider is taken to have consented, and a renter may keep the pet where the provider has consented in writing or the Tribunal has made an order permitting it. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If a timely application was made, the documents do not establish whether the allergy would justify refusal: that depends on the evidence and the Tribunal’s assessment of the relevant facts. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes: all three points are covered. The hardest one, the three-week application, is met by 'Three weeks is 21 days, so if no such Tribunal application was made within that 14-day period, the Act says consent is deemed.' The answer also states the 14-day deemed-consent rule and gives the next step: 'Ask the agent in writing whether the residential rental provider made a Tribunal application within 14 days of receiving your request.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes: none of the failing claims is made. The answer says the provider "must not unreasonably refuse" and is "taken to have consented unless, within 14 days after receiving the request, it applies to the Tribunal," so the refusal is not treated as final and the Tribunal application falls to the provider, not the renter; it also says the Act "does not make the owner's allergy an automatic ground for refusal" and that whether it justifies refusal "depends on the evidence and the Tribunal's assessment."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the only required document with its version, "Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, dated 13 October 2026", and links to 97-109aa115, which is the version in force on 15 October 2026. Every rule it applies (the 14-day deemed consent, the Tribunal application under s 71D, and the matters the Tribunal may consider) is cited to that version, and no other version is relied on.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
## Law in force on 1 October 2025

The applicable document is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 110, dated 6 August 2025**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

A landlord may give a notice to vacate if the premises are, immediately after the termination date, **to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) The Act does **not** say that a notice automatically ends merely because a particular buyer withdraws. It also does not require the landlord to withdraw the notice when a sale falls through. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The notice is withdrawn only by a **written notice of withdrawal**, signed by both the person who gave the notice and the renter. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) Therefore, unless that has happened, the notice remains on foot—but whether it is **valid and enforceable** depends on facts not provided, including whether the landlord still genuinely intends to sell or offer the premises for sale with vacant possession, and whether the notice met the Act’s requirements. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The notice must be in the relevant prescribed form, state the reason and termination date, and—because this is a sale notice—be accompanied by approved documentary evidence supporting the reason. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do

- **Do not assume the notice is cancelled.** Ask the landlord in writing either to provide a signed withdrawal notice or to confirm the proposed sale and the basis on which the notice remains valid. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- You may apply to the Tribunal to challenge the validity of a sale notice **within 30 days after it was given**, and the Tribunal can determine whether it is valid. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- If the termination date has passed, the landlord cannot obtain a possession order merely because the notice exists: the Tribunal must be satisfied that the landlord was entitled to give it, that it **has not been withdrawn**, and that you remain in possession after the termination date. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf)

So, **the buyer pulling out does not by itself cancel the notice**. You may still have to leave if the notice is valid and a possession order is made, but the documents do not provide enough facts to determine whether this particular notice is valid.

must-mention.reason: No. The answer covers withdrawal only by a written notice signed by both parties, the 30-day VCAT challenge, and the dependence on the sale ground and its evidence, but it never states the minimum 60-day notice period.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the three failure conditions is asserted: the answer says the opposite of the first two ('the buyer pulling out does not by itself cancel the notice' and withdrawal requires a notice 'signed by both the person who gave the notice and the renter'), and it states no minimum notice period at all, since the only period mentioned ('within 30 days after it was given') is the deadline for a Tribunal challenge.

version-cited.reason: No — the answer correctly names 'Authorised Version 110, dated 6 August 2025', but it also relies on version 098 (link 97-109aa098) for the possession-order rule that the Tribunal must be satisfied the notice 'has not been withdrawn'. Version 098 was not in force on 1 October 2025, and that rule is presented as current law, so deleting it would change the answer's substance.

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
## Law in force on 1 October 2025

The applicable documents retrieved are:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version v110, dated 6 August 2025** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version v004, dated 1 July 2025** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

Under section 44 of the Act, a rental provider must give at least **60 days’ notice in the prescribed form** of a proposed rent increase. A rent increase that breaches this requirement is **invalid**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) The prescribed form says that the rental provider must use **Form 5**, and that a valid notice is required for all rent increases. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, an ordinary email saying that the rent will increase is not enough **unless the email actually contained the prescribed Form 5 information and was delivered in a permitted way**. Form 5 allows delivery by email only **if you have consented to receive notices by email**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) On the facts given—no official rent-increase notice—you do **not** have to pay the higher rent yet. The documents do not require the agent to negotiate or accept a negotiated amount. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

The Act says the increase cannot take effect until the required notice period has run. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) However, the retrieved Regulations’ Form 5 says **at least 90 days’ notice**, which conflicts with section 44’s **60-day** wording. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) The retrieved documents do not explain that conflict, so they do not allow the exact minimum notice period to be stated with certainty. In either event, the higher rent cannot start merely because the agent emailed you about it.

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent to provide a valid **Form 5 notice**, including:

- the amount of the increase;
- how it was calculated;
- the proposed start date; and
- the required information about your right to seek an investigation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

You should also check whether you previously consented to receive formal notices by email, and whether the email contained all Form 5 particulars. Those facts determine whether it might itself qualify as the prescribed notice. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. The answer covers every point. It says the increase requires notice in the prescribed Form 5. It states that section 44 requires 'at least 60 days' notice'. Its doubt about whether the minimum might be 90 days still leaves at least 60 days either way. It says that without the form 'you do not have to pay the higher rent yet' and that a non-compliant increase is 'invalid'. It also gives a reasonable next step: 'Ask the agent to provide a valid Form 5 notice'.

must-not-say.reason: No — instead of settling on 60 days, the answer puts forward a 90-day minimum as a possibly governing alternative, saying "the retrieved Regulations' Form 5 says at least 90 days' notice" and that the documents "do not allow the exact minimum notice period to be stated with certainty."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version v110, dated 6 August 2025' (link 97-109aa110) and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version v004, dated 1 July 2025' (link 21-3sra004), and relies on no other version.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
## Law in force on 15 October 2026

The applicable Act was **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The applicable regulations document was **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 5, dated 25 November 2025**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

- You **must notify the rental provider in writing as soon as practicable** after becoming aware of damage to the rented premises. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The regulations’ renter-information summary also expressly says that, when damage occurs, the renter must notify the rental provider in writing. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)
- Skirting-board damage caused by a dog is not identified in the retrieved documents as an urgent repair. The Act’s rule allowing a renter to arrange repairs applies to **urgent repairs**, and only after the renter has taken reasonable steps to arrange for the rental provider or agent to do them immediately but cannot get them to do so. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- Repairs—urgent or non-urgent—must be done by a **suitably qualified person**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)
- The Act does not say that you may secretly arrange a non-urgent repair without notifying the rental provider. It does require notice of the damage, and the Tribunal may consider whether the provider was notified and given a reasonable opportunity to carry out the repair, and whether you have documentary evidence of the repair. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The retrieved documents contain **no rule about the owner’s or rental provider’s property insurance**, including whether your repair would affect an insurance policy or claim. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do

Notify the rental provider or agent **in writing now**, describe the damage, and say that you want to arrange a suitably qualified repairer. Ask for written agreement about the repairer, scope of work and cost, and keep photographs, the quote, invoice and proof of payment. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

You should not assume that a quick private repair removes your obligation to report the damage or prevents the rental provider from considering the damage when the tenancy ends. The retrieved documents do not state who ultimately pays for this particular dog damage, nor do they determine the insurance consequences; those issues depend on facts not provided and, for insurance, on the relevant policy.

must-mention.reason: No. The answer never says that the renter is responsible for damage they or their pet cause (as opposed to fair wear and tear) or that they must leave the home in the same condition; it instead says 'The retrieved documents do not state who ultimately pays for this particular dog damage,' which hedges the point. The other three points are covered: written notice as soon as practicable, the documents not settling the insurance question, and the next step of notifying in writing and agreeing on the repair.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the prohibited claims appear: the answer rejects a quiet repair ('You must notify the rental provider in writing as soon as practicable'), states no insurance outcome as fact ('The retrieved documents contain no rule about the owner's or rental provider's property insurance' and 'nor do they determine the insurance consequences'), and never says the renter must pay the owner's insurance excess.

version-cited.reason: No: the answer names the Act correctly as 'Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026', but it relies on 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 5, dated 25 November 2025' (link 21-3sra005) for applied rules, such as written notice of damage and repairs by a suitably qualified person, when the version in force on 15 October 2026 was Authorised Version No. 009 dated 30 June 2026.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
## Law in force on 1 March 2023

The applicable documents are:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version v101, dated 7 September 2022** [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version v002, dated 1 June 2022** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

Those documents **do not prescribe a minimum number of electrical circuits** for a rental. They therefore do not, on the material retrieved, require the rental to have separate circuits for the kettle and heater. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The Regulations’ electrical-safety minimum standard was stated to apply **“on and from 29 March 2023”**, not on 1 March 2023. It requires power outlets and lighting circuits to be connected to compliant circuit breakers and residual-current devices, but it does **not specify how many circuits** there must be. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The Act does require the rental provider to maintain the premises **in good repair** and in a **reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation**, with repairs or works carried out by a suitably qualified person. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can ask for

Give the rental provider or agent **written notice** describing the tripping—particularly that the breaker trips when the kettle and heater operate together—and ask them to arrange a **qualified electrical inspection and any necessary repair**. The Act requires a renter to give written notice as soon as practicable after becoming aware of a breakdown of facilities, fixtures, furniture or equipment provided by the rental provider. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

You can ask specifically for:

- an electrician to determine whether the circuit, breaker, outlets or wiring are defective or overloaded; and
- whatever repair or electrical alteration is reasonably necessary to keep the premises in good repair and reasonably fit for occupation. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

The documents do **not** establish that the breaker tripping is automatically an “urgent repair”, so whether the urgent-repair procedure applies depends on facts not provided—such as whether there is a danger, loss of essential power, burning, sparking or other electrical fault. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

If the provider does not carry out a **non-urgent repair within 14 days** after your written notice, you may apply to the Director to investigate; you may also apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring specified non-urgent repairs after the statutory conditions are met. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both required points are covered. On the number of circuits, the answer says the documents "do not prescribe a minimum number of electrical circuits" for a rental. On the next step, it tells the renter to give "written notice" and ask for a "qualified electrical inspection and any necessary repair." It also says urgent-repair treatment depends on whether there is danger, such as burning or sparking. That matches the rubric's "urgent if the fault is dangerous" point.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
## Law in force on 15 October 2026

The applicable **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version v115, dated 13 October 2026**, does **not specifically say that coin-operated washing machines are allowed or prohibited**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

However, the Act requires a rooming-house operator who **charges an amount for services** to:

- give the resident a **separate schedule of the amount for the services before the resident moves in**; and
- give an **itemised account showing the resident’s individual use** if the resident uses those services. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The applicable **Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023, Authorised Version v002, dated 1 December 2024**, require a washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents, based on the rooming house’s maximum capacity. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf) The Regulations do **not state that using that washing machine must be free**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf)

**Therefore:** the documents do not establish a blanket ban on charging for the machines. A charge may be covered as a charge for a service, but whether your operator has complied depends on facts not provided—particularly whether you were given the required service-charge schedule before moving in and whether you receive an itemised account showing your use. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can ask

Ask the operator in writing for:

1. the separate schedule for the laundry charge that should have been provided before you moved in; and  
2. an itemised account showing your individual use of the washing machines. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The documents do not provide a specific rule about the amount that may be charged for ordinary rooming-house laundry services.

must-mention.reason: Yes: all four points are covered. The answer says the Regulations require 'a washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents'. It says 'The Regulations do not state that using that washing machine must be free.' It says the operator must 'give the resident a separate schedule of the amount for the services before the resident moves in.' It gives as a next step: 'Ask the operator in writing for... the separate schedule for the laundry charge that should have been provided before you moved in.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the three failure statements is asserted. The answer says the documents "do not establish a blanket ban on charging for the machines", so it does not claim the machines must be free. It sets out charge rules ("a separate schedule of the amount for the services before the resident moves in" and "an itemised account showing the resident's individual use"), so it does not claim there are no rules on charges. Its only limit is that the documents give no rule on the amount charged, and it never claims a cost cap applies to all rooming houses.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version v115, dated 13 October 2026' (link 97-109aa115) and 'Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023, Authorised Version v002, dated 1 December 2024' (link 23-10sra002), and relies on no other version.

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
## Law in force on 1 October 2025

The applicable documents are:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 — Authorised Version v110, 6 August 2025** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 — Authorised Version v004, 1 July 2025** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved law does **not** expressly prohibit an advertisement from displaying a photograph that appears to show mould. It also does not contain a rule saying that the photograph must be removed or that the property cannot be advertised solely because mould appears in the image. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

However, a rental provider or agent covered by section 30E must not induce someone to enter the tenancy by misleading or deceptive conduct, or by a false or misleading representation about the premises’ characteristics. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) Whether displaying the photo is misleading would depend on facts not given—for example, whether the photo accurately represents the premises at the time of advertising, whether the mould is still present, and what the advertisement says or implies. Section 30E expressly applies where the provider or agent is **not acting in trade or commerce**; the retrieved documents do not explain the rule that would apply instead where they are acting in trade or commerce. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The minimum standard is that **each room must be free from mould and damp caused by, or related to, the building structure**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) Therefore, an apparent mould patch in a bedroom may indicate non-compliance, but the photo alone does not establish all parts of that legal test. The documents contain no rule stating that a photograph is conclusive proof, or setting out an evidentiary test for proving non-compliance. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

## What the renter can ask or do

Before entering the agreement, ask the rental provider or agent:

1. **Whether the premises comply with the rental minimum standards**; and [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
2. Whether the provider has received, in the previous **3 years**, a repair notice relating to mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

Those are prescribed matters that must be disclosed before entering a residential rental agreement. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) The provider must also disclose other prescribed information before entry, including information required by section 30D of the Act. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

If the renter enters and the premises do not comply with the minimum standards **on or immediately after the occupation day**, the renter may request urgent repairs to bring them into compliance. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) A photo can be useful supporting material—particularly if dated and identifying the room—but, on these documents alone, it is not automatically proof that the minimum standard has been breached. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: the output states the minimum standard that 'each room must be free from mould and damp caused by, or related to, the building structure'; it says 'the photo alone does not establish all parts of that legal test' and 'it is not automatically proof that the minimum standard has been breached'; and it gives next steps (ask the provider/agent about compliance and prior mould repair notices, and request urgent repairs after occupation).

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer makes neither prohibited claim, stating that the law does "not expressly prohibit an advertisement from displaying a photograph that appears to show mould" and that "the photo alone does not establish all parts of that legal test."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997 — Authorised Version v110, 6 August 2025' (link 97-109aa110) and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 — Authorised Version v004, 1 July 2025' (link 21-3sra004), and every rule it applies comes from those versions, not from any earlier or later one.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
## Law in force on 15 October 2026

The applicable Act is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, dated 13 October 2026**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The applicable regulations are **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009, dated 30 June 2026**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

If your friend is a **sub-tenant**, or you have assigned or purported to sub-let all or part of the premises without the rental provider’s consent, the rental provider may give **you** a notice to vacate. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) That notice must specify a termination date at least **14 days after the notice is given**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

However, the retrieved provisions do **not** say that you can use that 14-day rule yourself to evict your friend. They also do not provide a specific procedure for removing a friend who is merely an additional occupant rather than a sub-tenant. Whether your arrangement is a sub-let depends on facts not given—particularly whether your friend pays you rent, has exclusive use of part of the premises, or has some other occupancy arrangement.

You should therefore:

1. **Determine whether the arrangement was a sub-let or another type of occupancy.** The documents provided do not define that distinction or give a separate removal process for an ordinary occupant.  
2. **Do not use force or personally remove anyone.** The regulations state that a rental provider cannot personally use force to remove a renter; forcible eviction may only be carried out by Victoria Police under a VCAT possession order and warrant. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) The documents do not expressly state whether that rule applies to a friend who is not a renter.  
3. If the rental provider gives you a notice to vacate, it must be properly served; a notice to vacate may be delivered personally, sent by registered post, or given electronically in accordance with the Electronic Transactions (Victoria) Act 2000. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The prescribed form must state the reason, the relevant Act section, the termination date, and specific details supporting the reason. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)  
4. You may challenge such a notice at VCAT if, for example, it was not properly given, the reason or information is incorrect, or you believe it was given because you exercised your rights. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents do not say what notice, if any, you must give your friend, or whether you can require them to leave immediately.

must-mention.reason: No — the missing point is that sub-letting needs the landlord's written consent. The first point is covered: 'particularly whether your friend pays you rent, has exclusive use of part of the premises'. The answer only says the rental provider may give a notice to vacate if you 'purported to sub-let... without the rental provider's consent'. That implies consent matters, but it never states that sub-letting requires consent, and it never mentions that the consent must be written.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer asserts none of the four failing claims: it attaches the 14-day period only to a rental provider's notice to the renter and says the documents "do not say what notice, if any, you must give your friend"; it advises "Do not use force or personally remove anyone"; it never says the friend has no rights; and it never says the friend can apply to VCAT to be added to the lease.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, 'Authorised Version 115, dated 13 October 2026' (link 97-109aa115), and relies only on in-force versions, including the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 'Authorised Version 009, dated 30 June 2026' (21-3sra009).

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
## Law on 1 November 2019

The retrieved documents do **not** include the Victorian residential-tenancy legislation version in force on **1 November 2019**. The closest Act retrieved is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version v089, dated 4 December 2019**, which is later than your date. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf) I therefore cannot reliably state that its rules applied on 1 November 2019.

In that later version, the Act says:

- A renter must give written notice as soon as practicable about damage or a breakdown of landlord-provided fixtures. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
- For non-urgent repairs, after written notice and 14 days without repairs, the renter may apply to the Director for an investigation or to the Tribunal for repair orders. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
- A notice to vacate without a reason generally required at least **120 days’ notice** under the later version. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
- The later version specifically made a notice under section 263 ineffective if it was given in response to exercising, or proposing to exercise, a right under the Act; it did **not** state that every type of notice to vacate was retaliatory merely because it followed a repair request. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

Because that is a later version, I cannot apply those rules to your 1 November 2019 situation.

## What you should check

The retrieved documents do not provide the applicable 1 November 2019 version or its prescribed notice form, so they do not establish:

- which statutory section the notice should rely on;
- the required notice period for your particular month-to-month agreement;
- whether that type of notice could be challenged as retaliatory;
- the time limit or procedure for challenging it.

The facts that would decide the issue include **the exact date and version of the Act in force on 1 November 2019, the notice’s stated reason or section, the termination date, whether it was in the prescribed form, and what repair request or other right you exercised**. The retrieved documents do not contain enough information to answer those points for that date.

must-mention.reason: No. The 60-day VCAT challenge point is missing entirely. The 120-day no-reason notice and the retaliatory-notice rules appear only for a later version (v089, 4 December 2019), and the answer then says 'I cannot apply those rules to your 1 November 2019 situation'. That hedge leaves the reader unable to tell whether those rules applied on the user's date.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the landlord needed to give a reason; its only related statement, 'A notice to vacate without a reason generally required at least 120 days' notice under the later version', describes a notice period in a later version of the Act, not a deadline for challenging at VCAT. On deadlines, it says only that the documents do not establish 'the time limit or procedure for challenging it.'

version-cited.reason: No. The answer never names Authorised Version No. 088 (dated 2 July 2019), the version in force on 1 November 2019. Instead it names 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version v089, dated 4 December 2019', which is a later version, and its cited link (21-3sra002) points to the Regulations, not the Act. It also sets out rules from v089 (the 14-day repair process, the 120-day notice and section 263 retaliation), which counts as relying on them despite its caveat that they may not apply.

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
## Law in force on 1 October 2025

The applicable document retrieved is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version v110, dated 6 August 2025**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

It prohibited a rental provider or agent from:

- advertising or offering premises other than at a **fixed amount of rent**; and
- **soliciting or inviting** an offer higher than the advertised rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

It also prohibited false or misleading representations about rent in advertising. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, if the agent or provider encouraged applicants to offer more than the advertised price, that may breach the rental-auction provisions. A different applicant’s unsolicited higher offer, by itself, is not enough on the retrieved text: the prohibition is on soliciting or inviting the higher offer. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) The later retrieved Regulations say more about unsolicited offers, but they are dated **25 November 2025** and are not the version in force on your stated date, so they cannot be applied here.

The later higher listing may also be relevant if the original advertisement was false or misleading about the rent. However, the documents do not establish that merely changing the advertised rent after your application is unlawful, nor do they require the agent to accept your application, explain why it was rejected, or tell you whether another applicant offered more. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The Act’s provision on misleading or deceptive conduct applies where conduct induces a person to enter a residential rental agreement. On the facts given, you did not enter an agreement, so the documents do not establish that this provision applies to the alleged false “withdrawn” email. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do and save

You can raise the suspected breach with the rental provider or agent and ask them to confirm in writing:

1. that you did not withdraw your application;
2. who recorded it as withdrawn and when;
3. the rent at which the property was originally advertised;
4. when and why the rent was changed; and
5. whether applicants were invited or encouraged to offer more than the advertised rent.

The retrieved Act notes that VCAT can make orders in proceedings concerning a contravention of the misleading-conduct provision, but the retrieved documents do not state the procedure or available remedy for the rental-auction or misleading-advertising provisions. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

Save the original advertisement showing the price, the application and its submission time, the email saying you withdrew, all later correspondence, screenshots or PDFs showing the higher listing and their dates, and any message or witness account indicating that a higher offer was solicited or invited. The retrieved documents do **not** prescribe an evidence list or impose a specific evidence-preservation duty, so these are practical records to keep rather than statutory requirements.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered. (1) Relisting: 'the documents do not establish that merely changing the advertised rent after your application is unlawful.' (2) Soliciting is banned: the answer says the Act prohibits 'soliciting or inviting' offers above the advertised rent. (3) Unsolicited offers: 'A different applicant's unsolicited higher offer, by itself, is not enough on the retrieved text: the prohibition is on soliciting or inviting the higher offer.' (4) The withdrawn email, the hardest point: 'the documents do not establish that this provision applies to the alleged false "withdrawn" email.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the three prohibited claims is asserted, and the answer rejects each of them. It says "the documents do not establish that merely changing the advertised rent after your application is unlawful" and "A different applicant's unsolicited higher offer, by itself, is not enough," and it notes the law does not "require the agent to accept your application."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Act with its in-force version, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version v110, dated 6 August 2025' (with a 97-109aa110 link), and mentions the later Regulations dated 25 November 2025 only to say they 'cannot be applied here', without applying any rule from them.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
## Law in force on 15 October 2026

The applicable document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, dated 13 October 2026**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

A rental provider **must not unreasonably refuse** consent to keep a pet. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The provider is taken to have consented unless, **within 14 days after receiving the request**, they apply to the Tribunal for an order that refusing consent is reasonable. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

You sent the approved form **three weeks ago**, so the 14-day period has passed. If the agent received the request on the owner’s behalf and the owner did **not** apply to the Tribunal within those 14 days, the owner is taken to have consented. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) A refusal by the agent alone does not replace that statutory process. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The Act does **not** say that an owner’s allergy automatically justifies refusal, and it does not make the owner’s frequency of visiting decisive. The Tribunal may consider the type of pet, the character and nature of the apartment, its fixtures and fittings, whether another Act permits refusal, prescribed matters, and any other relevant matter. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The retrieved documents do not state how an allergy or rare visits must be assessed.

## What you can do

Ask the agent in writing:

1. whether the owner applied to the Tribunal **within 14 days** of receiving your request; and  
2. if not, acknowledge that consent is taken to have been given under section 71C(2). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Do **not** assume consent if the owner did make a timely Tribunal application: the documents do not say whether that application is pending or what its outcome is. The Tribunal can permit the dog or, if satisfied refusal is reasonable, order that consent be refused and the dog excluded. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. The output says 'The provider is taken to have consented unless, within 14 days after receiving the request, they apply to the Tribunal.' It applies this to the three-week timeline: 'the 14-day period has passed... if the owner did not apply to the Tribunal within those 14 days, the owner is taken to have consented.' It also gives the next step to 'Ask the agent in writing... whether the owner applied to the Tribunal within 14 days.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes: none of the failing claims is asserted. The answer says "A refusal by the agent alone does not replace that statutory process," puts the Tribunal application on the owner ("unless, within 14 days after receiving the request, they apply to the Tribunal"), and says "The Act does not say that an owner's allergy automatically justifies refusal."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, dated 13 October 2026' and cites only that in-force version (link 97-109aa115) for every rule it applies, with no reliance on an earlier or later version.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
## Law in force on 1 October 2025

The applicable Act is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110, dated 6 August 2025**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) The applicable form Regulations are **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 004, dated 1 July 2025**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf)

A landlord may give a notice to vacate for sale if, **immediately after the termination date, the premises are to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) The Act does **not** say that a notice automatically ends merely because a particular buyer withdraws, and it does not provide a special rule for that situation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

However, the notice is withdrawn only if the landlord gives a **written notice of withdrawal signed by the landlord and signed by the renter**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) Therefore, unless that has happened, the notice has not been formally withdrawn—but whether it is still **valid and enforceable** depends on facts not given, including:

- whether the landlord still intended to sell or offer the property for sale with vacant possession immediately after the termination date; [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- whether the notice was in the prescribed form, stated the reason and required details, and included supporting documentary evidence; [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf)
- whether the notice gave at least **60 days** before the termination date; and [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- whether the notice was given within the statutory **14-day** period after a relevant sale contract or satisfaction of its conditions, where that rule applied. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can do

You can ask the landlord, in writing, to confirm that the notice is withdrawn and provide the required signed notice of withdrawal. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) If the landlord does not do so, you may challenge the notice at VCAT; for a notice under the sale provision, the application must generally be made within **30 days after the notice was given**, or it may be challenged when the landlord applies for a possession order. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

Do **not** assume that the landlord can physically remove you. If you remain after the termination date, the landlord must apply to VCAT for a possession order, and only Victoria Police can carry out a forcible eviction under a warrant for possession. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf)

**Bottom line:** the buyer pulling out did not, on the documents provided, automatically cancel the notice. You may still have to leave if the notice is valid and VCAT makes a possession order, but the missing facts above determine whether the sale notice remains valid.

All four points are covered: the answer ties validity to the sale ground and its evidence ('offer the property for sale with vacant possession', 'supporting documentary evidence', and the '14-day period after a relevant sale contract'), states the 60-day minimum, says the notice is withdrawn only by a 'written notice of withdrawal signed by the landlord and signed by the renter', and gives next steps (ask for the signed withdrawal, or apply to VCAT 'within 30 days after the notice was given').

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
## Law in force on 1 October 2025

The relevant versions are:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110, dated 6 August 2025** [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 004, dated 1 July 2025** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

For a residential tenancy, the rental provider must give the renter **at least 60 days’ notice in the prescribed form** of a proposed rent increase. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) The Regulations require the rental provider to use **Form 5**, which must state the current rent, new rent, start date, and calculation method. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

An ordinary email saying that the rent will increase is not enough if it is not a valid prescribed notice. The Act says that a rent increase made contrary to these requirements is **invalid**. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) Therefore, on the facts given, you do **not** have to pay the higher rent merely because the agent emailed you or refused to negotiate. You should continue paying the existing rent. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The documents do not state a separate date from which a renter must pay where no valid notice has been given. They do state that a valid Form 5 must give at least 60 days’ notice and specify the proposed start date. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) Accordingly, the higher rent cannot validly start before the required notice period has elapsed after a valid notice is given; the exact date cannot be calculated without knowing when a valid notice is served.

You should check:

- whether the email was actually the prescribed Form 5;
- whether you had consented to receiving notices by email, since Form 5 permits email delivery where the renter has consented; [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- whether the tenancy is fixed-term, because rent generally cannot be increased during the fixed term unless the agreement provides for an increase; [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- whether rent has already been increased within the previous 12 months, since increases cannot occur at intervals of less than 12 months. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The documents do not say that a failed negotiation itself changes the rent or creates a rent increase. If the agent later gives a valid notice and you believe the proposed rent is excessive, you may apply in writing to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria within **30 days after the notice is given** for an investigation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered: it requires 'at least 60 days' notice in the prescribed form' (Form 5); it treats the email as an invalid notice ('a rent increase made contrary to these requirements is invalid... you do not have to pay the higher rent merely because the agent emailed you'); and it gives next steps ('continue paying the existing rent' and applying to Consumer Affairs Victoria once a valid notice arrives).

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the fail conditions is asserted: the answer says "you do **not** have to pay the higher rent merely because the agent emailed you," gives "at least 60 days' notice" as the minimum, says the increase "cannot validly start before the required notice period has elapsed after a valid notice is given," and states that "Form 5 permits email delivery where the renter has consented."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110, dated 6 August 2025' (link 97-109aa110) and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 004, dated 1 July 2025' (link 21-3sra004), and every rule it applies is sourced only from these versions.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
## Law in force on 15 October 2026

The applicable documents are:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 009, dated 30 June 2026** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The dog damage is damage to the rented premises. You must give the owner—or rental provider—**written notice as soon as practicable** after becoming aware of it. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Regulations also state that renters must avoid damaging the premises and notify the rental provider in writing when damage occurs. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The Act permits a renter to arrange repairs themselves only where the repairs are **urgent**, the renter has first taken reasonable steps to have the rental provider or agent carry them out immediately, and they cannot get them to do so. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Regulations require repairs—urgent or non-urgent—to be done by a **suitably qualified person**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The documents do not say that chewed skirting boards are urgent repairs. They describe urgent repairs as including failure or breakdown of essential services or appliances supplied by the rental provider, such as hot water, cooking, heating or laundering appliances. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) Whether these boards fall within the urgent-repair procedure therefore depends on facts not provided—particularly the nature and severity of the damage and whether it creates an immediate safety or essential-service problem.

### Can you fix it without telling the owner?

**You should not keep it secret.** You have a statutory obligation to notify the rental provider in writing as soon as practicable. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) If the skirting-board damage is non-urgent, the retrieved documents do not give you a right to arrange the repair yourself without notifying the owner; the self-arranged repair procedure in section 72 is specifically for urgent repairs. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

You can notify the owner in writing, offer to arrange a suitably qualified repairer promptly, and keep photographs, quotes, invoices and proof of payment. The Act expressly requires documentary evidence of a repair to be considered in a non-urgent-repair proceeding. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

### Could it affect the owner’s insurance?

**The retrieved tenancy-law documents contain no rule about whether your repair or non-disclosure would affect the owner’s insurance.** They do not state any insurance-notification requirement, policy condition, or consequence for the owner’s insurance. The effect on insurance depends on the relevant insurance policy and facts that are not provided; it cannot be determined from these documents.

must-mention.reason: No — the answer never says the renter is responsible for damage they or their pet cause (as distinct from fair wear and tear) or that they must leave the home in the same condition; it only says renters 'must avoid damaging the premises and notify the rental provider in writing.' The written-notice, insurance and next-step points are covered.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer rejects a quiet repair ("You should not keep it secret"), declines to state an insurance outcome ("it cannot be determined from these documents"), and says nothing about the renter paying the owner's insurance excess.

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names both required documents in the versions in force on 15 October 2026, the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 'Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026' (link 97-109aa115) and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 'Authorised Version No. 009, dated 30 June 2026' (link 21-3sra009), and it relies on no other version.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
## Law in force on 1 March 2023

The relevant document is **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, S.R. No. 3/2021, Authorised Version v002, dated 1 June 2022**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

- The retrieved rules **do not prescribe a minimum number of electrical circuits** for a rental, and do not require power points to be divided across a particular number of circuits. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
- The electrical rental minimum standard requiring **all power-outlet and lighting circuits** to be connected to compliant circuit breakers and residual-current devices applied **“on and from 29 March 2023”**—so it was not yet the applicable minimum-standard date on 1 March 2023. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
- The regulations did require the rental provider to arrange an **electrical safety check of all electrical installations, appliances and fittings they provided**, every **2 years**, conducted by a licensed or registered electrician. If no check had occurred within the previous 2 years when you moved in, it had to be arranged as soon as practicable. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can ask for

You can make a **written request for the date of the most recent electrical safety check**. The provider must give you that date in writing on request. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf) You can also ask the provider to arrange a licensed or registered electrician to investigate why the breaker trips when the kettle and heater operate together and to rectify any electrical defect identified. The retrieved rules do **not**, however, state that the provider must install an additional circuit merely because those appliances trip the breaker. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

Whether the provider is already in breach depends on facts not given: **when the last electrical safety check occurred, whether the breaker and other electrical equipment are safe and compliant, and whether the tripping results from a defect or simply the circuit’s load**. The retrieved documents do not provide a specific rule classifying this particular tripping as an urgent repair or specifying a guaranteed remedy. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Both points are covered. The answer states that the rules 'do not prescribe a minimum number of electrical circuits', and it gives next steps: 'make a written request for the date of the most recent electrical safety check' and ask the provider to arrange an electrician to investigate and 'rectify any electrical defect identified'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says neither forbidden thing: it states the rules "do not prescribe a minimum number of electrical circuits" and that the RCD/circuit breaker standard applied "on and from 29 March 2023"—so it was not yet the applicable minimum-standard date on 1 March 2023.

version-cited.reason: No. The answer cites 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, S.R. No. 3/2021, Authorised Version v002, dated 1 June 2022', which is the version in force on 1 March 2023. However, it never names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version No. 101), which the rubric requires for urgent repairs (s 3(1)) and safety-related duties (s 68A(1)), so a required document is missing.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
## Law in force on 15 October 2026

The applicable documents are:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, dated 13 October 2026** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023, Authorised Version 2, dated 1 December 2024** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

**Yes, the documents allow the possibility of charging for laundry services, but they do not expressly say that coin-operated washing machines may or may not charge a fee.** The rooming-house standards require, from 26 February 2024, a washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents, based on the maximum number the house can accommodate. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) They do **not** say that using the machine must be free. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If the operator charges an amount for laundry services, section 109 requires the operator to:

- give you a **separate schedule of the amount for the services before you take up residency**; and
- if you use the service, give you an **itemised account showing your individual use**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf)

The documents do not state a specific maximum coin charge for an ordinary private rooming-house operator, and they do not state that a coin-operated machine is automatically unlawful. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The special rule allowing a service charge for laundry facilities where use cannot practicably be measured applies to **Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency**, not generally to every rooming-house operator. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do

Ask the operator in writing for:

1. the separate schedule showing the laundry-service charge that was provided before your residency began; and  
2. an itemised account showing your individual laundry use. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf)

You can also check your residency agreement and any documents given to you before moving in. On the documents provided, whether the particular coin charge is lawful depends on facts not supplied—especially **who operates the rooming house, whether the charge is for a service, and whether the required schedule and itemised account were provided**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. The output covers all four points: it states that the standards require a washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents, and that they 'do not say that using the machine must be free'. It says section 109 requires 'a separate schedule of the amount for the services before you take up residency', and it advises asking the operator in writing for 'the separate schedule showing the laundry-service charge that was provided before your residency began'.

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
## Law in force on 1 October 2025

The retrieved **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version v004, dated 1 July 2025** was the relevant Regulations version provided for that date. It states that **each room must be free from mould and damp caused by, or related to, the building structure**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

However, the retrieved **Residential Tenancies Act 1997** is **Authorised Version v111, dated 25 November 2025**, which is later than the date in your question. I therefore cannot use it to determine the advertising rule on 1 October 2025. The retrieved documents do not provide the Act version in force on 1 October 2025, so they do not establish whether displaying the photos breached the advertising provisions. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

## Is the photo enough to prove non-compliance?

**No—not by itself, on these documents.** The minimum standard is not simply “no visible mould”: it concerns mould or damp **caused by, or related to, the building structure**. A photograph that appears to show mould may be relevant evidence, but it does not establish from the documents alone what the substance is, how extensive it is, or whether it is structurally caused. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

## What the prospective renter can do or ask

The retrieved documents do not state a specific step that a prospective renter may take about mould shown in an advertisement, nor do they set an evidentiary test for proving non-compliance. You can ask the rental provider or agent:

- whether the substance is mould or damp;
- what caused it; and
- whether it will be remedied before occupation.

Whether the premises meet the standard would depend on facts not provided—particularly whether there is actually mould or damp and whether it is caused by, or related to, the building structure. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. The answer states the mould and damp standard ('each room must be free from mould and damp caused by, or related to, the building structure'). It says the photo alone is not enough ('No—not by itself, on these documents'). It gives a next step ('You can ask the rental provider or agent... whether it will be remedied before occupation').

must-not-say.reason: Yes — neither failing assertion is made: on the photo, the answer says "No—not by itself, on these documents", and on advertising, it declines to say the ad breached any rule, stating the documents "do not establish whether displaying the photos breached the advertising provisions", so it never claims a ban applied on 1 October 2025.
