question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
## Law in force on 15 October 2026

This answer is based on **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version v115, dated 13 October 2026** [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version v009, dated 30 June 2026** [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

The Act says you **must not assign or sub-let all or part of the rented premises without the residential rental provider’s written consent**. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) An unauthorised assignment or sub-letting is invalid unless VCAT has decided that consent was not required. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

However, the documents do **not** say that every friend who moves in is automatically a sub-tenant or that you must notify the agent merely because a friend is staying there. Whether this was an assignment or sub-letting depends on facts not given—particularly whether your friend pays you rent, has exclusive possession of part or all of the premises, and whether you still live there.

If it was an unauthorised sub-let or assignment, the rental provider may give **you** a notice to vacate under section 91ZV, with a termination date at least **14 days after the notice is given**. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The prescribed notice form is addressed to the renter who is a party to the rental agreement, and the reason must include the relevant section and specific details. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents do **not** provide a procedure for you to personally evict a friend who is merely an occupant or guest. They also do not authorise you to use force or change the locks. For a renter who does not leave after a notice, the prescribed information says that only Victoria Police may carry out a forcible eviction, and only under a VCAT possession order and warrant. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- Ask the friend to leave and put that request in writing; the documents do not prescribe a particular notice period or form for this situation.
- If the arrangement was a sub-let, ask the rental provider or agent for **written consent** or ask whether they will agree to end it. The provider must not unreasonably withhold consent. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- If consent is withheld and you believe that is unreasonable, you may apply to VCAT for a determination that consent is not required. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- Tell the agent or rental provider what happened and ask for written confirmation of the arrangement they require; the documents do not state that contacting the agent is, by itself, the required method for removing the friend.

The key missing facts are whether your friend pays rent, whether they have exclusive possession, whether you remain living at the property, and what your rental agreement says about additional occupants.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
## Law in force on 15 October 2026

The applicable document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, dated 13 October 2026**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

You must request consent using the form approved by the Director and give it to the residential rental provider. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The provider **must not unreasonably refuse** consent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Most importantly, the provider is **taken to have consented** unless, within **14 days** after receiving the request, they apply to the Tribunal for an order that refusing consent is reasonable. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Since you say you sent the request three weeks ago, the 14-day period has apparently passed.

The owner’s allergy is **not automatically a valid refusal** under the Act. The Act does not say that the owner’s frequency of visits decides the issue. Instead, the Tribunal may consider matters including the type of pet, the character and nature of the apartment, its appliances, fixtures and fittings, whether refusal is permitted under another Act, prescribed matters, and any other relevant matter. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

### What you can do

- Ask the agent in writing whether the residential rental provider applied to the Tribunal within the 14-day period, and request confirmation of the application date. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- If no application was made within 14 days, the provider is taken to have consented under section 71C(2). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- If an application was made, the Tribunal can decide whether refusal is reasonable and may order that you are permitted to keep the dog. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The documents do not state whether an allergy, by itself, is reasonable grounds for refusal. That would depend on facts not provided, including whether the request was received, whether it used the approved form, whether a Tribunal application was made within 14 days, and the circumstances of the alleged allergy and the apartment. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. The hardest one, that consent is taken as given after three weeks unless a VCAT application was made, is covered by 'Since you say you sent the request three weeks ago, the 14-day period has apparently passed' together with 'If no application was made within 14 days, the provider is taken to have consented under section 71C(2).' The answer also states the 14-day deemed-consent rule and gives the next step of asking the agent in writing whether a Tribunal application was made.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer says none of the three, since it states the provider is "taken to have consented" unless they themselves "apply to the Tribunal" within 14 days, and that the allergy is "not automatically a valid refusal."

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
## Law in force on 1 October 2025

The applicable document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 110, dated 6 August 2025**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

A landlord may give a notice to vacate under **section 91ZZB** if, immediately after the termination date, the premises are to be **sold or offered for sale with vacant possession**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) The Act does **not** say that a notice automatically ends or becomes invalid merely because a prospective buyer later withdraws. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The notice is withdrawn only by a **written notice of withdrawal** signed by both the person who gave the notice and the renter. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) Therefore, unless it is formally withdrawn or successfully challenged, the notice remains on foot; however, the landlord cannot simply remove you themselves. A possession order requires, among other things, that the landlord was entitled to give the notice and that it has not been withdrawn. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

Whether you ultimately have to leave depends on facts not provided, including:

- whether the notice was valid when given under section 91ZZB;
- whether it was in the prescribed form, signed, stated the reason and termination date, and included the required documentary evidence;[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- whether the termination date has passed; and
- whether the landlord has obtained a possession order. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do

You can ask the landlord to give you a formal written withdrawal. If the notice was given within the last **30 days**, you may apply to the Tribunal to challenge its validity; the application must be made on or before the hearing of the landlord’s possession-order application and within 30 days after the notice was given. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved Act does not state that the landlord must withdraw the notice solely because the buyer pulled out, so the documents do not establish that you can remain without considering the notice’s validity and any Tribunal process. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: No: the answer never states the 60-day minimum notice period. It also does not distinguish a planned sale with vacant possession from a signed contract of sale, although it does cover written withdrawal signed by both parties and the 30-day Tribunal challenge.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the three failing claims is asserted: the answer rejects automatic cancellation ('The Act does not say that a notice automatically ends or becomes invalid merely because a prospective buyer later withdraws'), requires joint withdrawal ('a written notice of withdrawal signed by both the person who gave the notice and the renter'), and gives no minimum notice period (its '30 days' is the window for a Tribunal challenge).

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the only required document with its in-force version, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 110, dated 6 August 2025', and every rule it applies is cited to that version via the 97-109aa110 link, with no reliance on any other version.

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
## Law in force on 1 October 2025

The applicable documents are:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 110, dated 6 August 2025** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 004, dated 1 July 2025** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider must give you **at least 60 days’ notice, in the prescribed form**, of a proposed rent increase. The notice must state the increase, how it was calculated, and your right to seek an investigation. A rent increase that breaches these requirements is **invalid**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The prescribed notice is **Form 5**. It must include, among other things, the current and new rent, the start date, the calculation method, and the rental provider’s details. It may be sent by email **only if you had consented to email delivery**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, **you do not have to pay the higher rent merely because the agent emailed that the rent was going up or refused to negotiate**. If that email was not a valid Form 5 notice—or you had not consented to receiving the notice by email—the increase is invalid. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) The documents do not say that negotiation or refusal to negotiate itself changes the rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

If there is a valid notice, the higher rent can start **no earlier than 60 days after the notice was given**, on the start date stated in the notice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) Since you have not provided the email date, the proposed start date, or whether you consented to email notices, the exact date cannot be determined.

You can ask the agent or rental provider to give you the prescribed Form 5 notice. If you receive one and consider the proposed rent excessive, you may apply **in writing within 30 days after the notice is given** to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria for an investigation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered: the answer names the prescribed Form 5, requires at least 60 days' notice, and gives next steps (ask for Form 5, then seek a Consumer Affairs Victoria investigation within 30 days). The hardest point is covered by 'you do not have to pay the higher rent merely because the agent emailed that the rent was going up... If that email was not a valid Form 5 notice... the increase is invalid.' This wording is conditional, but it is not hedged so far that a reader could not tell which way it falls.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: none of the failing claims are made, since the answer says "you do not have to pay the higher rent merely because the agent emailed," requires "at least 60 days' notice," says the rent can start "no earlier than 60 days after the notice was given" rather than from the email date, and allows email delivery "only if you had consented to email delivery" rather than saying it can never be emailed.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions: 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 110, dated 6 August 2025' (link 97-109aa110) and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 004, dated 1 July 2025' (link 21-3sra004). Every rule it applies is sourced only from these in-force versions.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
## Law in force on 15 October 2026

The applicable documents are:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 — Authorised Version 115, dated 13 October 2026**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 — Authorised Version 009, dated 30 June 2026**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The Act requires a renter to give the rental provider **written notice as soon as practicable after becoming aware of damage** to the rented premises. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Regulations likewise state that, where damage occurs, the renter must notify the rental provider in writing. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, you should **not arrange the repair secretly without telling the owner or agent**. The documents do not provide a general right to conceal damage and repair it without notice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The Regulations say that **only a suitably qualified person may carry out urgent or non-urgent repairs**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) The Act allows a renter to arrange **urgent** repairs only after taking reasonable steps to have the rental provider or agent carry them out immediately and being unable to get them to do so; the renter must then give seven days’ written notice of the repairs and cost. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The retrieved documents do not specifically say whether chewed skirting boards are an urgent repair. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do

You can:

1. **Notify the owner or agent in writing now**, describing the damage and providing photographs. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
2. Ask whether they want to arrange the repair or consent to you arranging it.
3. If they authorise you to arrange it, use a **suitably qualified person** and keep the quote, invoice and photographs. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
4. If the work is treated as an urgent repair, the Act’s renter-arranged-repair procedure requires the steps above; the Regulations state that reimbursement for renter-arranged urgent repairs is up to **$2,500**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The documents do not state that you can avoid notifying the owner because you are moving out soon. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## Insurance

The retrieved tenancy-law documents contain **no rule stating whether repairing the skirting boards would affect the owner’s property insurance**, and they do not set out any insurance-notification requirement or policy condition. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) That issue depends on the owner’s insurance policy and the facts of the damage and repair, which are not provided.

must-mention.reason: No. The answer covers written notice as soon as practicable, says the documents do not settle the insurance question, and gives next steps such as notifying in writing. However, it never says the renter is responsible for damage caused by them or their pet (as distinct from fair wear and tear), nor that the renter must leave the premises in the same condition.

must-not-say.reason: Yes, none of the fail conditions are asserted: the answer says "you should **not arrange the repair secretly without telling the owner or agent**", states insurance impact "depends on the owner's insurance policy and the facts of the damage and repair, which are not provided" rather than asserting an outcome, and never says the renter must pay the owner's insurance excess.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
## Law in force on 1 March 2023

The applicable document is **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, S.R. No. 3/2021, Authorised Version v002, dated 1 June 2022**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

That version **does not prescribe a minimum number of power circuits** for a rental. It therefore does not, on the retrieved material, require the rental provider to install additional circuits merely because the kettle and heater together trip the breaker. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

Its electrical minimum standard applied **“on and from 29 March 2023”**, requiring all power outlets and lighting circuits to be connected to compliant switchboard-type circuit breakers and residual-current devices. That date had not yet arrived on 1 March 2023. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The Regulations did require the rental provider to ensure an electrical safety check of electrical installations, appliances and fittings **provided by the rental provider** every two years, by a licensed or registered electrician. On request, the provider had to give you the date of the most recent check in writing. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can ask for

You can write to the rental provider asking them to:

- arrange an electrical safety check or inspection of the affected circuit by a licensed or registered electrician;
- investigate why the breaker trips when the kettle and heater operate together; and
- repair any defect identified by the electrician.

You can also request a copy of the most recent electrical safety-check record. The record must include the electrician’s details, date, results, required repairs and actions taken, and a copy must be provided within **7 days** after the provider receives your written request. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The documents do **not** say that you are entitled to a particular number of circuits, or that the provider must install a separate circuit or upgrade the electrical supply. Whether a repair or upgrade is required depends on the electrician’s findings, including whether the tripping indicates a defect or another electrical-safety problem. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. On circuits, the answer says the Regulations do 'not prescribe a minimum number of power circuits' and that 'the documents do not say that you are entitled to a particular number of circuits.' On next steps, it suggests writing to ask the provider to 'repair any defect identified by the electrician' and to request 'a copy of the most recent electrical safety-check record'. It also notes the provider had to give the date of the most recent check in writing on request. The rubric treats listed next steps as examples, so these are enough.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer asserts neither failure condition: it says the Regulations 'do[] not prescribe a minimum number of power circuits', and it says the circuit breaker and RCD standard applied 'on and from 29 March 2023' and 'That date had not yet arrived on 1 March 2023.'

version-cited.reason: No. The answer names only the 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, S.R. No. 3/2021, Authorised Version v002, dated 1 June 2022' and omits the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 101, which the rubric requires.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
## Law in force on 15 October 2026

The relevant Act is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, dated 13 October 2026**. The relevant standards are in **Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023, Authorised Version No. 002, dated 1 December 2024**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The standards require a rooming house to provide **one washing machine for every 12 or fewer residents**, based on the maximum number the house can accommodate. They require the machine to be in good working order, but **do not say that use must be free or prohibit a charge**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf)

The Act does not contain, in the retrieved provisions, a general rule specifically authorising or prohibiting an ordinary rooming-house operator from charging per use of a coin-operated washing machine. It does provide that, if an operator charges an amount for services, the operator must give the resident **a separate schedule of the amount before residency begins** and, when the resident uses the service, **an itemised account showing the resident’s individual use**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If the rooming house is operated by **Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency**, it may impose a service charge for laundry services or facilities only where it is **not possible or practicable to accurately measure each resident’s use**; the charge must not exceed the cost of providing the service or facility, and written notice is required when the charge is imposed or changed. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Ask the operator:

- what the washing-machine charge is for and how it was disclosed before you became a resident;
- for the required service-charge schedule and an itemised account of your use; and
- whether the operator is Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency, and, if so, how the charge complies with the limits above. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

On the documents provided, **there is not enough information to conclude that the coin-operated charge is lawful or unlawful**. The deciding facts include who operates the rooming house, whether the charge was disclosed before residency, and whether the operator provides the required schedule and itemised account. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered. question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
## Law in force on 1 October 2025

The retrieved **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 004, dated 1 July 2025**—the version available for the relevant date—sets the minimum standard that **each room must be free from mould and damp caused by, or related to, the building structure**. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved Act text is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 111, dated 25 November 2025**. Because that is later than 1 October 2025, the documents provided do not establish the Act’s exact Authorised Version in force on 1 October 2025. The later text nevertheless contains the relevant advertising rule: a provider or agent must not advertise premises unless, at the time of advertising, they **reasonably believe** the premises comply with the rental minimum standards. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

Accordingly:

- **They cannot lawfully advertise the premises if they know, or do not reasonably believe, that the bedroom has mould or structural dampness that means it fails the minimum standard.** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- The rule is about the provider’s or agent’s **reasonable belief at the time of advertising**; the retrieved documents do not say that every photograph showing something that looks like mould automatically makes an advertisement unlawful. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- **A photograph alone is not stated in the retrieved documents to be conclusive proof** that the premises fail the standard. The relevant questions include whether it is actually mould or damp, and whether it is caused by or related to the building structure. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

## What the renter can ask

A rental provider must disclose to a rental applicant **whether the premises comply with the rental minimum standards**. They must also disclose, from 31 December 2021, whether they received a repair notice in the previous three years concerning mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

The renter can therefore ask the provider or agent:

1. whether the premises comply with the mould-and-damp minimum standard; and  
2. whether they have received such a mould or damp repair notice in the previous three years. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

The documents do not provide a rule saying exactly what evidence is required to prove non-compliance, or that a photograph by itself is sufficient.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: the mould-and-damp standard is stated ('each room must be free from mould and damp caused by, or related to, the building structure'). The hardest point, the photo, is covered by 'A photograph alone is not stated in the retrieved documents to be conclusive proof'. A next step is given: 'The renter can therefore ask the provider or agent: whether the premises comply with the mould-and-damp minimum standard'.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
## Law in force on 15 October 2026

The applicable Act is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, dated 13 October 2026**. It says a renter must not **assign or sub-let all or part of the rented premises without the residential rental provider’s written consent**. An assignment or sub-letting without consent is invalid unless VCAT has decided that consent is not required. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The Act does **not** say that merely allowing a friend to stay is automatically a sub-let. Whether your arrangement with your friend amounts to an assignment or sub-letting depends on facts not provided—particularly whether your friend was given exclusive possession of all or part of the premises, and whether they paid you rent. The Act also refers to the **residential rental provider’s** written consent; it does not impose a separate requirement in the retrieved provision to notify the agent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If this was an unauthorised sub-let, the rental provider—not you—may give **you** a notice to vacate under section 91ZV. The notice must give at least **14 days** before its termination date. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you have to do to get your friend out

The retrieved documents do **not** provide a procedure for a renter to remove a friend or other occupant from the premises. They therefore do not establish that you can personally lock the friend out, remove their belongings, or use force.

You should first establish whether your friend is a sub-renter, co-renter, or merely an occupant, because the documents do not give the same answer for each situation. If the friend is a sub-renter, the arrangement is invalid without the rental provider’s written consent unless VCAT has ruled consent unnecessary. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If you need a formal notice or possession process, the retrieved **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009, dated 30 June 2026**, contain the prescribed **Form 6 notice to vacate**, but that form is for a rental provider or mortgagee giving notice to a renter—not for you requiring a friend to leave. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The documents do not state what your friend can do to challenge or resist your request to leave in this particular situation. They do state that a renter who receives a notice to vacate may challenge it at VCAT, and that only Victoria Police may carry out a forcible eviction under a VCAT possession order; those provisions concern the rental-provider/renter process, not a friend’s status as an occupant. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Both points are covered. The output says the arrangement 'depends on facts not provided—particularly whether your friend was given exclusive possession of all or part of the premises, and whether they paid you rent', which names deciding facts. It also states a renter must not sub-let 'without the residential rental provider's written consent'.

Its only fixed period, 'at least 14 days', applies to the rental provider's notice to the renter under s 91ZV, not to ending the friend's occupancy. It says the documents 'do not establish that you can personally lock the friend out, remove their belongings, or use force', and it never claims the friend has no rights or can simply apply to VCAT to be added to the lease.

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
Based on the law in force on 1 October 2025, here is how your situation is addressed under Victorian residential tenancy law.

### ⚖️ Law in Force on 1 October 2025
The applicable legislation is the ***Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Vic), Authorised Version v110 dated 6 August 2025** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

### 🛑 Can you challenge what happened?
Yes. The actions you described breach specific provisions of the Act:
* **Fixed Rent Requirement:** A rental provider or agent must advertise or offer premises with the rent stated as a fixed amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
* **Higher Offers:** It is illegal for a provider or agent to solicit or invite offers higher than the advertised rent, and they are also prohibited from accepting unsolicited offers that exceed the advertised amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
* **False Withdrawal Email:** Sending an email falsely claiming you withdrew constitutes misleading or deceptive conduct and a false representation concerning the agreement process, which is strictly prohibited [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

These are criminal offences under the Act, carrying penalties of 60 penalty units for individuals and 300 penalty units for corporations [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). You can challenge this by reporting the misleading conduct and illegal rent solicitation to **Consumer Affairs Victoria**. If you suffered financial loss as a direct result of this conduct, you may be able to apply to VCAT for orders regarding the contravention [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

### 📁 What should you save as evidence?
The Act does not prescribe a specific evidence checklist for this scenario. However, to prove the statutory breaches outlined above, you should immediately preserve:
* **Original Advertisement:** Screenshots or saved copies of the listing showing the fixed advertised price.
* **The False Email:** The email claiming you withdrew (keep full email headers and timestamps intact).
* **Proof of Your Application:** Submission confirmations, application receipts, or timestamped records proving you applied at the advertised price and never sent a withdrawal notice.
* **New Listing Details:** Screenshots of the property now listed at a higher rent.
* **Correspondence Logs:** All emails, texts, or call notes with the agent or provider regarding your application and the listing status.

*Note: If you need immediate guidance on lodging a complaint or preparing a VCAT application, contact a community legal centre or Consumer Affairs Victoria directly.*

Third, it says the false withdrawal email 'constitutes misleading or deceptive conduct... which is strictly prohibited' under the Act, which contradicts the point that no specific rental-law rule covers it. Only the ban on soliciting or inviting higher offers is correctly stated.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic)**, Authorised Version v115 dated 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), which is the law in force on your date:

### Can they refuse?
**No, the agent cannot unilaterally refuse your request, and their refusal is legally ineffective at this stage.** Under section 71C(1), a residential rental provider must not unreasonably refuse to consent to you keeping a pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

More importantly, because you submitted your official request three weeks ago (more than 14 days ago), the law treats the owner as having **already consented** to your dog. Section 71C(2) states that a provider is taken to have consented unless they apply to the Tribunal within 14 days of receiving your request [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Since the agent simply said "no" without taking this formal legal step within the two-week window, their refusal holds no weight under the Act.

### What about the owner's allergy and lack of visits?
While an owner's health or allergies can be a factor the Tribunal considers if they do apply (under the catch-all provision of *"any other matter the Tribunal considers relevant"*), the agent cannot use it as a blanket reason to deny your request without going through that formal process [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Furthermore, the fact that the owner "hardly ever visits" could also be considered by a tribunal under the *"character and nature of the rented premises"* or other relevant matters if the issue were formally contested [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do:
1. **Notify the agent in writing:** Inform them that under section 71C(2) of the Act, their failure to apply to the Tribunal within 14 days means consent is legally deemed granted. 
2. **Apply to VCAT if necessary:** If they continue to block you from keeping the dog, you can apply to the Tribunal (VCAT) for an order permitting you to keep the pet on the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. The hardest one, three weeks having passed, is met by "because you submitted your official request three weeks ago (more than 14 days ago), the law treats the owner as having already consented," read with the stated rule that consent is deemed "unless they apply to the Tribunal within 14 days." Notifying the agent in writing is a reasonable next step.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the three failure conditions is asserted. The answer says the refusal is not final ("their refusal is legally ineffective at this stage"), presents VCAT as optional ("Apply to VCAT if necessary... you can apply"), and treats the allergy as only a factor ("an owner's health or allergies can be a factor the Tribunal considers").

This matches the version in force on 15 October 2026, and every rule applied (ss 71C(1), 71C(2), and the Tribunal factors) is sourced from that version, with no reliance on an earlier or later version.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
**Direct Answer**
Yes, you are still legally required to vacate the property by the termination date specified in the original notice. Under Victorian residential tenancy law, a notice to vacate given on the grounds of selling the property does not automatically lapse or become invalid if the buyer pulls out or the sale falls through [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf).

**The Law in Force on 1 October 2025**
The governing legislation is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Vic), Authorised Version No. 110, dated 6 August 2025 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Under this framework, a notice to vacate remains a valid and enforceable legal document until it is formally cancelled by the landlord. 

**How the Notice Can Be Cancelled**
For the notice to be withdrawn, the landlord must issue a formal "notice of withdrawal" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf). This document must meet strict procedural requirements:
* It must be in writing [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf).
* It must be signed by the person who gave the original notice (the landlord) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf).
* It must also be signed by you (the tenant/renter) to whom the notice was given [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf).

Because the buyer has pulled out but your landlord has not provided this formal written withdrawal, the original notice to vacate remains in full force. The fact that decides whether you still have to leave is simply whether this specific withdrawal document has been executed and signed by both parties [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf).

**What You Can Do**
1. **Request a Formal Withdrawal:** Immediately ask your landlord to provide the formal written notice of withdrawal now that the sale has been cancelled. 
2. **Challenge the Notice at VCAT:** If the landlord refuses to withdraw the notice, you have the right to challenge its validity at the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT). You can do this if you believe the reason given (sale of property) is factually incorrect or unsupported by evidence—for example, if the premises are no longer actually for sale [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). This application must generally be made within 30 days of the notice being given [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Request More Time:** If you cannot move out by the termination date, you can ask VCAT for an extension if vacating on that date would cause you significant hardship [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 
4. **Know Your Rights During Eviction:** Even if you do not leave voluntarily, your landlord cannot personally use force to remove you [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Only Victoria Police can carry out a forcible eviction, and only after obtaining a warrant from VCAT [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: No. The answer covers withdrawal in writing signed by both parties and gives next steps (a formal withdrawal request, a VCAT challenge within 30 days). However, it never says the outcome depends on the ground stated in the notice and its evidence (planned sale with vacant possession vs a signed contract), and it never mentions the 60-day minimum notice period.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the three failure conditions is asserted: the answer rejects automatic cancellation ('does not automatically lapse or become invalid if the buyer pulls out'), requires the withdrawal to be signed by both the landlord and 'by you (the tenant/renter)', and states no minimum notice period at all (the only period mentioned, '30 days', is a VCAT application deadline).

The core holding that the notice does not lapse, the withdrawal-notice signing requirements and the 30-day VCAT challenge period are all cited to 97-109aa089 (Version 89 of the Act). The steps on challenging at VCAT, seeking more time and forcible eviction are cited to 21-3sra005 (Regulations Version 005, dated November 2025), a later version than the in-force Version 004. Deleting the material sourced from these versions would remove most of the answer's substance.

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021** (specifically version `rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf`, which was updated on 1 July 2025 and is the version in force on your date), here is how the law applies to your situation:

### Do you have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
**No, you do not have to pay the higher rent.** Under Victorian tenancy law, **a valid notice of a proposed rent increase is required for all rent increases** [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 

Because you never received an official notice, your agent's informal email does not satisfy this legal requirement. Your rent remains at the current amount until a compliant statutory notice is properly served and the mandatory notice period has passed (which was at least 60 days under the version of the regulations in force on 1 October 2025 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)). 

### What you can do or ask
1. **Request the official form:** Ask your agent for the official **Form 5 (Notice of Proposed Rent Increase to Renter of Rented Premises)**. A valid notice must include the specific method used to calculate the increase and cannot exceed that calculated amount [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 
2. **Continue paying your current rent:** Keep paying your existing rent amount until you receive a valid notice and the required notice period expires.
3. **Challenge the increase:** If the agent insists on the increase without providing a valid notice, or if they attempt to evict you for "non-payment" of the unnotified amount, you can apply to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria for a free investigation or directly to VCAT to have the increase declared invalid or excessive [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 

*(Note: While the regulations were later updated in November 2025 to extend the notice period to 90 days [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf), the fundamental requirement that a valid, formal notice must be provided remains unchanged.)*

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered: the answer names the official Form 5, says the notice period was 'at least 60 days' on 1 October 2025, says the agent's 'informal email does not satisfy this legal requirement' so the rent stays the same, and gives a next step to 'Keep paying your existing rent amount'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says "No, you do not have to pay the higher rent" and gives "at least 60 days under the version of the regulations in force on 1 October 2025". It mentions 90 days only for the later November 2025 version, and its point about the "informal email" does not claim a notice can never be sent by email.

It also relies on a version that was not in force on 1 October 2025: it says 'a valid notice of a proposed rent increase is required for all rent increases', and sets out the Form 5 calculation-method requirement and the VCAT/Consumer Affairs challenge step, citing the link '21-3sra005', which is Regulations version 005 from November 2025. It should have cited version 004.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
Based on the Victorian residential tenancy laws in force on 15 October 2026, specifically the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version v115 dated 13 October 2026)** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (Authorised Version v005 dated 25 November 2025)** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf), here is how your situation is handled:

**1. Can you fix the skirting boards without telling the owner?**
No, you cannot. Under section 72AA of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, you are legally required to give written notice to your residential rental provider (the owner) as soon as practicable after becoming aware of any damage to the rented premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The standard tenancy agreement also explicitly states that where damage occurs, you must notify the rental provider in writing [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 

**2. Who should fix it?**
Because your dog caused the damage, this is considered tenant-caused damage rather than a maintenance issue for the landlord. However, under the standard tenancy agreement, only a suitably qualified person may carry out repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Skirting board damage does not qualify as an "urgent repair" (which covers essential services like hot water, cooking, or heating failures) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). For non-urgent repairs, the rental provider is responsible for carrying them out in a reasonable time after receiving your notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). You cannot simply arrange for a quick fix without informing the owner first, as doing so would breach your obligation to report the damage. 

**3. Would it affect the owner's insurance?**
The retrieved documents do not contain any information or rules regarding how tenant repairs might affect the landlord's property insurance. 

If you need to proceed with the repair, you should notify the owner in writing immediately and discuss who will cover the cost of the qualified tradesperson needed to fix the skirting boards.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997** (Vic), Authorised Version v115 dated 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), and the **Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023**, Authorised Version v002 dated 1 December 2024 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf), here is how the law applies to your situation on 15 October 2026:

**Yes, rooming house operators are allowed to charge you for using coin-operated washing machines**, but whether they can legally do so depends entirely on who owns the building and whether they have followed specific disclosure rules. 

Here is what the law requires depending on your operator:

### 1. If you live in a privately owned rooming house
Under section 109 of the Act, if a private rooming house operator charges an amount for services (which includes laundry facilities), they are permitted to charge you, but they must meet two strict requirements [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf):
* **Pre-move-in disclosure:** They must provide you with a separate schedule of the amount relating to those services *before* you take up residency in the room [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
* **Itemised accounts:** If you use any of those services, they must provide you with an itemised account showing your individual use of the services [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

### 2. If you live in a Homes Victoria or registered housing agency rooming house
Under section 109A of the Act, these specific operators may impose a service charge for laundry facilities, but only if it is not possible or practicable to accurately measure your individual use of the machine [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Furthermore:
* The charge **must not exceed the actual cost** of providing the service or facility to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
* They must give you written notice if they impose or change this charge [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

### 3. The operator must still provide the washing machines
Regardless of who owns the building, the *Rooming House Standards Regulations 2023* require that rooming house operators provide at least one washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents (based on the maximum capacity) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). The law mandates they *provide* the facility, but it does not prohibit them from charging a fee for its use.

### What decides your situation?
To determine if you are being charged correctly, the deciding facts are:
* **Who is the operator?** (Private owner vs. Homes Victoria/registered agency)
* **Did they give you a schedule of service charges before you moved in?**
* **Do they provide itemised accounts when you use the machines?**
* **If it is a government/agency property, does the charge exceed the actual cost of providing the laundry service?**

If these conditions are not met, you may have grounds to dispute the charge. For private operators, failing to provide the required schedule or itemised account breaches section 109 of the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). For Homes Victoria or registered agencies, charging above cost or failing to give notice breaches section 109A [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). You can apply to the Tribunal (VCAT) to have these charges withdrawn or varied.

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021** (S.R. No. 3/2021), Authorised Version dated 1 July 2025, which was in force on 1 October 2025:

No. Under Clause 8 of Schedule 4 of the Regulations, each room in the rented premises must be "free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). A photograph can at best show the presence of a substance that looks like mould, but it cannot prove the *cause* of that mould. To prove a breach of this standard, it would need to be established that the mould is "caused by or related to the building structure" rather than resulting from other factors (such as tenant lifestyle, poor ventilation, or water leaks unrelated to the structure) [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Because the cause is a necessary fact for determining compliance, a photo alone is insufficient proof.

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997** (Authorised Version No. v110, dated 6 August 2025), which was in force on 1 October 2025 [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf):

### Can you challenge what happened?
Yes, the law prohibits the conduct you described. Under this version of the Act:
* Rental providers and their agents **must not solicit or invite an offer higher than the advertised rent** for the premises [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
* They **must not make false or misleading representations** in relation to the rent for the premises [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
* They **must not induce a person to enter into a residential rental agreement by engaging in conduct that is misleading or deceptive**, including making false representations concerning the rent payable under the agreement [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

If the agent falsely claimed you withdrew to re-list at a higher price and subsequently accepted a higher offer, this may constitute a breach of these provisions. You can apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) for orders regarding contraventions of these sections [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### What should you save as evidence?
The retrieved documents do not provide a specific statutory evidence checklist for this exact scenario. However, to support a challenge regarding the advertised rent and misleading conduct, you should preserve:
* Proof of the original fixed advertised rent (e.g., screenshots or links to the listing).
* Your original rental application submitted at that advertised price.
* The email falsely stating that you withdrew.
* Any subsequent advertisements, emails, or records showing the property was re-listed at a higher price or that another offer above the advertised amount was accepted.

### What the documents do not cover
The Act does not explicitly state whether you can force the provider to rent to you, automatically invalidate the new listing, or undo the rental application process itself. It strictly regulates the advertising and solicitation of rent amounts, as well as misleading conduct during the application phase [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

The *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (Authorised Version v005, dated 25 November 2025) also explicitly state that where damage occurs, you must notify the rental provider in writing [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**Can you get someone to fix it yourself?**
Generally, no. You are only permitted to arrange for repairs yourself if they qualify as "urgent repairs" (such as a burst pipe or broken lock) and you have first taken reasonable steps to get the owner or their agent to do them immediately without success [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations strictly limit urgent repairs to failures of essential services like hot water, cooking, heating, or laundering [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Skirting board damage is considered non-urgent. For non-urgent repairs, the rental provider is responsible for carrying out the work in a reasonable time after you notify them [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

The retrieved documents do not contain any rules or information regarding how tenant-caused damage or repairs would impact the property owner's insurance.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
**Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs?**
No. The *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (Schedule 4, clause 9) does not specify a minimum number of electrical circuits that a rental property must have [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). 

**What can you ask for?**
While the law doesn't mandate a specific number of circuits, it does require that all power outlets and lighting circuits be connected to a switchboard-type Circuit Breaker complying with AS/NZS 3000 "Electrical Installations" and a switchboard-type Residual Current Device (RCD) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). A breaker that trips whenever you run two appliances together indicates an overloaded circuit or faulty wiring.

Under the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Vic), your rental provider has a legal duty to maintain the premises in good repair and ensure it is fit for habitation [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Because of this, you can:
1. **Ask your rental provider to arrange for a licensed electrician to inspect the circuit.** You can request that they either redistribute your appliances across different circuits or upgrade the wiring/breaker if it is faulty or undersized.
2. **Request repairs through the proper channels.** If the electrical fault poses a safety risk (e.g., risk of fire or shock), you can classify this as an urgent repair under the Act [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If it is not an immediate safety hazard, you can still request it as a standard maintenance repair.

*(Note: The specific minimum standard requiring RCDs and compliant circuit breakers commences on 29 March 2023, but your provider's general duty to maintain the property in good working order applies immediately [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).)*

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. The answer says the regulations do 'not specify a minimum number of electrical circuits'. It also gives the next step: 'If the electrical fault poses a safety risk (e.g., risk of fire or shock), you can classify this as an urgent repair under the Act... you can still request it as a standard maintenance repair.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer denies any minimum ('does not specify a minimum number of electrical circuits'), and although it says the law 'does require' compliant circuit breakers and RCDs, its note says this standard 'commences on 29 March 2023', so it does not claim the standard already applies on 1 March 2023.

It also applies rules from those later versions, such as the RCD and circuit breaker standard and the urgent repairs and maintenance duties.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
Based on the law in force on 15 October 2026, **yes**, your rooming house operator is allowed to charge you to use coin-operated washing machines. 

The relevant laws are the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Authorised Version No. v115 dated 13 October 2026) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and the *Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023* [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf).

Here is what the law says about your situation:

**1. Charging for Laundry Services**
The Act explicitly allows a rooming house operator to charge residents for services, which includes laundry facilities [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents do not prohibit coin-operated machines, nor do they mandate that laundry must be free or included in your rent. 

However, if the operator charges you for these services, they are legally required to:
* Provide you with a separate schedule of the amount relating to those services **before** you take up residency [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* If you use any of those services, provide you with an itemised account showing your individual use of them [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**2. Requirement to Provide Washing Machines**
While the operator can charge for the service, they are still required to provide the equipment under the Rooming House Standards Regulations 2023 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). Specifically, the operator must provide at least one washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents based on the maximum number of residents the house can accommodate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do:**
* Ensure you have received a schedule of service charges prior to moving in. 
* If you use the machines, request an itemised account showing your individual usage as required by law [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* If the washing machines are broken or not provided in the required ratio (one per 12 residents), you can raise this with the operator as a breach of the Rooming House Standards [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes: all four points are covered. The answer states the operator must provide 'at least one washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents', says the documents do not 'mandate that laundry must be free', says a separate schedule of service charges must be given 'before you take up residency', and gives the next step 'Ensure you have received a schedule of service charges prior to moving in.'

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997** (No. 109 of 1997, Authorised Version dated 25 November 2025) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021** (S.R. No. 3/2021, Authorised Version dated 25 November 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), here is how the law applies to your situation on 1 October 2025:

### 1. Are they allowed to advertise it like that?
The legislation does not explicitly ban a rental ad from showing a photo that merely *looks like* it has mould. However, under section 65B of the Act, a provider or their agent **must not advertise premises to let unless** at the time of advertising they **"reasonably believe the premises comply with the rental minimum standards"** [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

If the photo clearly depicts a condition that violates the minimum standards, it could be very difficult for the provider to demonstrate that they held a "reasonable belief" that the property was compliant when they advertised it [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### 2. Is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
To prove a breach of the mould standard, a photo alone is likely **not enough** on its own. The rental minimum standard states that *"Each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure"* [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 

Therefore, the deciding fact is not just the *presence* of mould, but whether it is **"caused by or related to the building structure"** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). A photograph cannot prove the *cause* of the mould (for example, distinguishing between structural dampness and mould caused by tenant lifestyle). The retrieved documents do not specify what additional evidence would be required to legally prove this cause. 

*(Note: If you need to determine if a specific photo constitutes misleading advertising or proves a breach of standards, the provider's actual knowledge at the time of listing and independent expert reports on the cause of the dampness would be the deciding facts, which are not covered in these documents.)*

must-mention.reason: No: the answer covers the mould and damp standard ('caused by or related to the building structure') and says a photo alone likely isn't enough, but it gives no next step for the user, such as asking the agent, checking at the inspection, requesting urgent repairs, or ending the agreement before moving in. Its mention of 'independent expert reports' is framed as a deciding fact not covered by the documents, not as advice to act on.

It cites the Regulations as "Authorised Version dated 25 November 2025" (link 21-3sra009, version 009) instead of Version No. 004 dated 1 July 2025. It applies rules from those later versions as the law.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
Based on the law in force on 15 October 2026, specifically the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (No. 109 of 1997, Authorised Version v115 as at 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (S.R. No. 3/2021, Authorised Version v009 as at 30 June 2026) [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), here is what applies to your situation:

**What the documents say about removing a guest**
The retrieved documents do not contain any rule or procedure for how a tenant must terminate a guest's or unauthorised occupier's stay. The Act and Regulations only govern the legal relationship between landlords (rental providers) and tenants (renters), not private arrangements between tenants and their guests.

**What the documents *do* say about your situation**
While the documents do not tell you how to evict your friend, they do set out a rule that applies to you as the tenant: under clause 32 of the Regulations, you must not sub-let or assign any part of the premises to another person without the rental provider's written consent [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If your friend is effectively living there as a subtenant, allowing them to stay without telling your agent breaches this rule. The landlord may give you a notice to vacate for this breach [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 

If your friend is merely staying temporarily as a guest and not paying rent or taking over the lease, it generally does not constitute subletting under these documents. However, because the provided legislation does not cover tenant-to-guest termination procedures, the documents do not contain the information you need to answer what steps you must take to end their stay.

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
Based on the law in force on 1 October 2025, here is how your situation is addressed under Victorian residential tenancy legislation:

### The Law in Force on 1 October 2025
Under the ***Residential Tenancies Act 1997*** (Authorised Version v110 dated 6 August 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf):
* **Fixed Rent Requirement:** A rental provider or agent must advertise or offer premises with a fixed rent amount; they cannot advertise without stating a specific price [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
* **No Bidding Above Advertised Rent:** It is prohibited for a provider or agent to solicit or invite any offer higher than the advertised rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
* **False/Misleading Conduct:** Providers and agents are strictly prohibited from making false or misleading representations about the rent, or using misleading/deceptive conduct to induce you to enter an agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

### Can You Challenge What Happened?
Yes. The agent's actions (falsely claiming you withdrew to manufacture urgency, soliciting higher offers, and relisting at a higher price) appear to breach the Act's prohibitions on misleading conduct and false advertising [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). 
* **Report to Consumer Affairs Victoria:** You can lodge a complaint with Consumer Affairs Victoria, which investigates residential tenancy breaches [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
* **Apply to VCAT:** The Act notes that the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) may make orders regarding contraventions of the misleading/deceptive conduct provisions [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

### Evidence to Save Immediately
To support a challenge, you should preserve the following:
1. **The Original Advertisement:** Screenshots or saved copies showing the property was listed at the fixed advertised price.
2. **The False Email:** The complete email chain falsely claiming you withdrew, including all headers and timestamps.
3. **Proof You Did Not Withdraw:** Any records showing you did not sign a written withdrawal notice (as valid withdrawals require specific formalities) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
4. **Evidence of the Price Hike & Higher Offers:** Screenshots of the new listing at the higher rent, and any communications or proof regarding the other person's offer above the advertised price.

*Note: The retrieved documents do not specify a detailed step-by-step VCAT application process for pre-agreement breaches beyond noting the Tribunal's power to make orders [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). For procedural steps, you should contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or seek legal advice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).*

It never says that accepting an unsolicited higher offer was not banned on this date. It also treats the false 'withdrawn' email as a breach of the Act's misleading-conduct provisions instead of saying no specific rental-law rule covers it. Only the ban on soliciting offers above the advertised rent is covered.
