question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997** (Vic), Authorised Version No. v115 dated 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), here is how the law applies to your situation:

### What the law says
Under section 71C of the Act, a residential rental provider (the owner or their agent) must not unreasonably refuse consent for you to keep a pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). However, because you sent your official request form **three weeks ago**, a specific "deemed consent" rule applies:

*   **Deemed Consent:** Section 71C(2) states that a residential rental provider is legally taken to have consented to your request unless they apply to the Tribunal within **14 days** of receiving it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Because three weeks (21 days) have passed and they did not apply to the Tribunal within that 14-day window, they are deemed to have consented.
*   **Unreasonable Refusal:** Even if they had applied to the Tribunal within the 14 days, section 71C(1) prohibits them from unreasonably refusing consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If a dispute went to the Tribunal, the Tribunal would consider factors like the nature of the apartment and "any other matter" (such as the owner's allergy) under section 71E(2)(f) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Given that the owner hardly ever visits, an allergy is likely to be considered an unreasonable ground for refusal.

### Can they refuse?
**No, they cannot validly refuse at this stage.** Because you sent your request more than 14 days ago and they did not apply to the Tribunal within that timeframe, the law treats them as having already consented [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do
You are legally permitted to keep your dog in the apartment. If the agent or owner continues to object, threatens eviction, or tries to enforce their refusal:
1.  Inform them in writing that under section 71C(2), they are taken to have consented because they failed to apply to the Tribunal within 14 days of receiving your request [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2.  If they continue to harass you or attempt to evict you, you can apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) to enforce your rights or seek remedies for their breach of the Act.

The answer states that the provider 'is legally taken to have consented to your request unless they apply to the Tribunal within 14 days of receiving it.' It applies this to the three-week timeline ('Because three weeks (21 days) have passed and they did not apply to the Tribunal within that 14-day window, they are deemed to have consented'). The hardest point is this one, because the answer assumes no VCAT application was made rather than framing it as a condition, but it still addresses the alternative ('Even if they had applied to the Tribunal within the 14 days...'). It also gives a reasonable next step: 'Inform them in writing that under section 71C(2), they are taken to have consented.'

It treats the allergy as a factor rather than decisive ("an allergy is likely to be considered an unreasonable ground for refusal"), and rests the outcome on deemed consent.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic)**, Authorised Version No. 110, dated 6 August 2025 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), here is how the law applies to your situation:

### Do you still have to leave?
No, you do not automatically have to leave just because the buyer pulled out, but the notice does not automatically expire either. Under the Act, a notice to vacate for sale (given under section 91ZZB) remains legally valid until it is formally withdrawn by your landlord [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf). 

### Why the notice hasn't expired
The law explicitly states that a notice to vacate is withdrawn **only** if a formal written notice of withdrawal is given, which must be signed by both you and your landlord [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf). The Act does not provide an automatic mechanism for the notice to lapse or become invalid simply because the sale contract was terminated. 

### What you can do
Because the original reason for the notice—that the premises are "immediately after the termination date to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession"—no longer applies, you have the right to challenge the validity of the notice [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

*   **Apply to VCAT:** You can apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) to challenge whether the notice is valid [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This application must be made within 30 days after the notice was given [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
*   **If you miss the 30-day window:** You can still raise the issue "on or before the hearing of an application for a possession order" if your landlord tries to evict you through the Tribunal [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). At that hearing, you would explain that the sale contract was terminated, meaning the premises are no longer intended to be sold with vacant possession as required by section 91ZZB [[11]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### Summary of next steps
1. Do not vacate based solely on the original notice without addressing its validity. 
2. Ask your landlord in writing to formally withdraw the notice since the sale has fallen through. 
3. If they refuse, file an application with VCAT to challenge the notice's validity (ideally within 30 days of receiving it) [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

*(Note: This information is based strictly on the statutory provisions retrieved for Victorian residential tenancy law as of your specified date.)*

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
Based on the law in force on 1 October 2025, **no, you do not have to pay the higher rent** based solely on an email from your agent. 

Under the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (S.R. No. 3/2021), v004 dated 1 July 2025** [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf), a valid written notice is strictly required for all rent increases [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). 

Here is how the law applies to your situation:

*   **The Notice Requirement:** For a standard residential rental agreement, the landlord must use the official **Form 5 (Notice of Proposed Rent Increase to Renter of Rented Premises)** to notify you [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). 
*   **The Timeframe:** The landlord must give you at least **90 days' notice** before any rent increase can take effect [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
*   **When the Higher Rent Starts:** Once you receive a valid Form 5, the new rent will apply from the **"Start date"** explicitly listed on that form. This start date cannot be sooner than 90 days after the notice is given to you [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). 

**What you can do:**
1.  **Request the official notice:** You can reply to your agent and state that under Victorian law, a valid rent increase requires an official Form 5 notice with at least 90 days' notice [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). 
2.  **Challenge the increase (if applicable):** If you eventually receive a valid Form 5 and believe the proposed increase is excessive, you can apply to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria to review it for free within 30 days of receiving the notice [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). You may also apply to VCAT to declare the amount excessive within 30 days after receiving the Director's report (or within 30 days after the notice if no report is provided) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

*(Note: The specific official form required depends on a fact you haven't provided: the type of tenancy agreement you hold. For example, standard residential rental agreements use Form 5, while rooming house agreements use Form 10 and caravan park site agreements use Forms 20 or 21. However, regardless of the tenancy type, a valid written notice is legally required before any increase can be charged [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).)*

must-mention.reason: No. The answer is missing the point that at least 60 days' notice is required: it says 'at least **90 days' notice**' and that the start date 'cannot be sooner than 90 days after the notice is given', which materially changes the meaning. It does cover the other points: Form 5, that the email alone does not make the higher rent payable, and next steps (requesting a Form 5 and applying to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria for review).

must-not-say.reason: No. The answer states a minimum notice period other than 60 days: "The landlord must give you at least **90 days' notice** before any rent increase can take effect."

No. 3/2021), v004 dated 1 July 2025' and never cites the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110, even though it applies rules from the Act (notice requirements and the Director/VCAT review steps under ss 44–45).

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
Based on the Victorian residential tenancy documents in force, here is the information regarding your situation as of 1 March 2023:

**Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs?**
No. The retrieved regulations and Acts do not specify a minimum number of electrical circuits or power points that a rental property must have. 

**What can you ask for?**
While the law does not mandate a specific number of circuits, you can take the following steps regarding the tripping breaker:

1. **Request Repairs under the Duty to Maintain:** The residential rental provider has a legal duty to maintain the rented premises in good repair [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). A circuit breaker that trips when normal appliances (like a kettle and heater) are used indicates an electrical fault or overload that should be addressed by a licensed electrician. You can formally request that they arrange for this electrical issue to be repaired.
2. **Request an Electrical Safety Check Record:** The provider must ensure an electrical safety check of all electrical installations is conducted every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). You can ask them to provide you with the date and results of their most recent safety check. If they have not had one done in the last 2 years, they are required to arrange one as soon as practicable [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Furthermore, if you make a written request, they must provide you with a copy of the most recent electrical safety check record within 7 days [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
3. **Note the Upcoming Electrical Safety Standard:** While not yet in force on your current date, be aware that a new minimum standard regarding electrical safety takes effect on **29 March 2023**. From that date forward, all power outlets and lighting circuits in the rental premises will be required to be connected to compliant switchboard-type circuit breakers and Residual Current Devices (RCDs) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). You can mention this upcoming requirement when discussing the electrical upgrades with your provider.

*Note: If the tripping breaker prevents you from using essential facilities or poses a safety risk, it may qualify as an urgent repair under the Act, but you should consult the specific definitions in Section 72 of the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 for that classification [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).* 

*(Citations correspond to the provided document set: [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) Schedule 4 cl. 9 of the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021; [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) Reg. 30 of the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021; [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf) Sch. 1 cl. 19 of the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021; [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) Section 68 & 72 of the Residential Tenancies Act 1997.)*

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. The answer says 'No. The retrieved regulations and Acts do not specify a minimum number of electrical circuits,' which covers the circuits point. For next steps it says 'You can formally request that they arrange for this electrical issue to be repaired' and 'You can ask them to provide you with the date and results of their most recent safety check.' It also notes the fault may qualify as an urgent repair if it poses a safety risk.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997** (Authorised Version No. 115 as at 13 October 2026) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and the **Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023** (Authorised Version No. 2 as at 1 December 2024) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf), here is how the law applies to your situation:

### Are they allowed to charge?
Yes. The retrieved documents do not contain any rule prohibiting rooming house operators from charging for the use of laundry facilities, including coin-operated washing machines. In fact, the Act explicitly contemplates that operators may charge for services [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

### What are the operator's obligations when charging?
If your operator charges you to use the washing machines, they must comply with the following requirements under section 109 of the Act:
* **Provide a schedule:** They must give you a separate schedule detailing the amount charged for these services *before* you take up residency [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **Provide an itemised account:** If you use the service, they must provide you with an itemised account showing your individual use of those services [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What are the standards for the machines?
Regardless of whether they charge, the operator is legally required to provide at least one washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents based on the maximum capacity of the rooming house [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf).

### Can you do anything about the cost?
* **If your operator is Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency:** They may impose a service charge for laundry facilities only if it is not possible to accurately measure your use, and the charge cannot exceed the actual cost of providing the service [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If they impose such a charge, you can apply to the Tribunal to have it withdrawn or varied [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **If your operator is private:** The documents do not provide specific rules on capping or regulating the price of coin-operated machines beyond the requirement to provide the schedule and itemised account mentioned above.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered: one machine per 12 residents, no rule against charging, a schedule given before moving in, and a next step. The next step is the hardest point; the answer never tells the user to check for or request the schedule, but it offers a reasonable alternative consistent with the law: 'you can apply to the Tribunal to have it withdrawn or varied' (for Homes Victoria or registered agency operators).

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says operators may charge ("Yes. ... the Act explicitly contemplates that operators may charge for services"), so it does not say the machines must be free. It also sets out rules on charges ("They must give you a separate schedule detailing the amount charged" and "an itemised account"), so it does not say there are none. Finally, it limits the cost cap ("the charge cannot exceed the actual cost") to operators that are "Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency" and not to all rooming houses.

The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions: 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version No. 115 as at 13 October 2026)' with link 97-109aa115, and 'Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023 (Authorised Version No. 2 as at 1 December 2024)' with link 23-10sra002. Every rule it applies comes from these in-force versions.

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
Based on the law in force on 1 October 2025, here is how the legislation addresses your questions:

### **1. Are they allowed to advertise it like that?**
Under section 65B of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (No. 109 of 1997), a rental provider or their agent must not advertise premises unless they **reasonably believe** the premises comply with the rental minimum standards at the time of advertising [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). 

The legislation does not explicitly ban photos that *look* like they show mould. However, if the property actually breaches the minimum standards, advertising it would be unlawful [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

### **2. What facts decide whether the advertising is allowed?**
To determine if the ad is lawful, two specific facts are needed:
* **The cause of the mould:** Under clause 8 of Schedule 4 of the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (S.R. No. 3/2021), the minimum standard only requires that rooms be "free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If the mould is structural, advertising the property would breach the standards. If it is cosmetic or caused by tenant behaviour (e.g., poor ventilation), it may not breach this specific standard.
* **The provider's reasonable belief:** The law hinges on whether the provider *reasonably believes* the premises comply with the standards at the time of the ad [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). 

### **3. Is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?**
The retrieved documents do not contain rules or guidance on what evidence is sufficient to legally prove that a property fails to meet the minimum standards. While the standard for mould is clearly defined as being free from structural dampness and mould [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), the documents do not specify whether a photograph alone constitutes adequate proof of a breach in a dispute or tribunal setting.

must-mention.reason: No. The answer covers the structural mould/damp standard ('free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure') and says the documents do not specify whether a photograph alone is adequate proof, but it gives no next step such as asking the agent, checking at the inspection, requesting urgent repairs or ending the agreement before moving in.

must-not-say.reason: No — the answer states the advertising ban applies on 1 October 2025, saying "a rental provider or their agent must not advertise premises unless they reasonably believe the premises comply with the rental minimum standards" and "if the property actually breaches the minimum standards, advertising it would be unlawful," although that rule does not apply on this date.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic)**, version 115, which was in force on 13 October 2026 (covering your date of 15 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021** (version in force from 30 June 2026) [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), here is exactly what you must do:

### 1. Issue a Notice to Vacate
Letting your friend move into part of the property without your permission constitutes assigning or sub-letting part of the premises without consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Under section 91ZV of the Act, you are entitled to give your renter a notice to vacate for this reason [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
*   You must use the official Notice to Vacate form and specify **section 91ZV** as the reason.
*   The notice must state a termination date that is **not less than 14 days** after the day you give the notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### 2. Apply to VCAT if They Do Not Leave
If your renter does not vacate by the termination date in the notice, you cannot force them out yourself. You must apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) for a possession order [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 
*   VCAT will hold a hearing to decide whether you were entitled to give the notice and whether it is "reasonable and proportionate" to make a possession order [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
*   If VCAT grants the order, only Victoria Police can carry out a forcible eviction by acting on a warrant for possession [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). You are strictly prohibited from personally using force to remove them [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

### Why This Is a Breach
Your standard residential rental agreement explicitly states that a renter `"must not assign (transfer to another person) or sub-let the whole or any part of the premises without the written consent of the rental provider"` [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Because your friend moved in without telling you (and thus without your written consent), this is a clear breach of both the Act and your agreement terms [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

*(Note: If your renter challenges the notice at VCAT, they may argue it was given improperly or for an incorrect reason. Ensure all details on the notice are accurate and specific to the situation.)*

The second point is covered by the quoted term that a renter 'must not assign... or sub-let the whole or any part of the premises without the written consent of the rental provider'.
